1-1.name: Basil the Great
1-1.desc: Archbishop of Caesarea, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs.
1-1.bio:
St. Basil the Great was born in Caesarea of Cappadocia in the fourth century, to a family of saints. Educated in Athens alongside his friend St. Gregory the Theologian, he set aside a brilliant secular career for the monastic life, and later served as Archbishop of Caesarea. He defended the divinity of Christ against Arianism, gave the Church the Divine Liturgy that bears his name, and organized one of the first great centers of Christian charity for the poor and the sick.

One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, he is honored as a father of monasticism and of Christian philanthropy. The Church commemorates him on January 1, a day beloved in Greek tradition, when the vasilopita is cut in his honor.

1-2.name: Seraphim of Sarov
1-2.desc: Beloved Russian monastic saint, wonderworker of Sarov.
1-2.bio:
St. Seraphim of Sarov, one of the most beloved saints of Russia, lived from the mid-eighteenth century until 1833. Entering the monastery of Sarov as a young man, he spent long years in seclusion in the forest in fasting, silence, and unceasing prayer, including, according to tradition, a thousand days and nights of prayer upon a rock.

In his last years he opened his cell to all, greeting every visitor as his joy with the paschal greeting that Christ is risen. Pilgrims beyond number received his counsel and healing. He taught that the aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit. His memory is kept on January 2.

1-3.name: Gordios
1-3.bio:
St. Gordios was a centurion of Caesarea in Cappadocia who lived in the time of the persecutions of the early fourth century. Withdrawing to the wilderness to live in prayer, he returned to the city during a great pagan festival and openly confessed Christ before the assembled crowds, knowing the cost. He was condemned and beheaded for his confession.

St. Basil the Great, a later bishop of the same city, honored his memory with a celebrated homily, and the Church has kept his name ever since as a model of fearless witness. He is commemorated on January 3.

1-4.name: Anastasia
1-4.bio:
St. Anastasia was a holy woman and martyr of Rome who gave her life for Christ during the persecutions of the early Church. The synaxaria preserve little of her story beyond her faithful confession, but her name, which means resurrection, has been cherished by the faithful as a sign of the hope for which she died.

Her endurance joins her to the great company of women martyrs whom the Church honors as brides of Christ. Her memory is kept on January 4.

1-5.name: Theopemptos
1-5.bio:
St. Theopemptos was a bishop who suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Tradition relates that his steadfastness under torture so moved a pagan sorcerer named Theonas that he too confessed Christ, was baptized, and shared in the crown of martyrdom.

Together the bishop and the converted sorcerer bear witness that the courage of the martyrs was itself a preaching of the Gospel. They are commemorated on January 5, the eve of Theophany.

1-6.name: Theophany
1-6.desc: The Epiphany — Baptism of the Lord Jesus Christ in the Jordan.
1-6.bio:
The Feast of Theophany, or Epiphany, commemorates the Baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ by St. John the Forerunner in the River Jordan. As Christ came up from the waters, the heavens opened, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, and the voice of the Father was heard — the first clear revelation of the Holy Trinity.

One of the twelve Great Feasts, Theophany celebrates the sanctification of the waters and of all creation. On this day the Church performs the Great Blessing of the Waters, and in Greek tradition the cross is cast into the sea and retrieved by swimmers as a blessing for the new year.

1-7.name: John the Baptist
1-7.desc: Feast of the Holy Forerunner and Baptist John.
1-7.bio:
On the day after Theophany, the Church gathers to honor St. John the Forerunner and Baptist, the greatest of the prophets, who was found worthy to baptize the Lord in the Jordan. Son of the priest Zacharias and the righteous Elizabeth, John lived in the wilderness in fasting and prayer, preaching repentance and preparing the way of the Lord.

Christ Himself said that among those born of women none had arisen greater than John. He completed his witness as a martyr, beheaded by Herod for rebuking his unlawful marriage. This Synaxis on January 7 is one of the most celebrated name days in the Greek world.

1-8.name: George the Chozebite
1-8.bio:
St. George the Chozebite was born on the island of Cyprus and became a monk of the monastery of Choziba, in the wild gorge on the road between Jerusalem and Jericho. Living in the seventh century, he embraced great austerity, humility, and unceasing prayer, and in time guided the brotherhood as a spiritual father.

His life, recorded by his disciple, preserves the memory of a gentle and severe ascetic in the tradition of the desert fathers of Palestine. He is commemorated on January 8.

1-9.name: Polyeuktos
1-9.bio:
St. Polyeuktos was a Roman soldier in Melitene of Armenia in the third century, and is honored as the first martyr of that city. Moved by the faith of his Christian friend Nearchos, he confessed Christ openly, refused to honor the idols, and was beheaded for the Lord he had only newly come to know.

His martyrdom sealed a friendship in Christ that the Church has remembered ever since, and a famous church in Constantinople later bore his name. He is commemorated on January 9.

1-10.name: Gregory of Nyssa
1-10.desc: Bishop of Nyssa, brother of Basil the Great.
1-10.bio:
St. Gregory of Nyssa was the younger brother of St. Basil the Great, born in Cappadocia in the fourth century to a family rich in saints. As Bishop of Nyssa he defended the Nicene faith against Arianism, endured exile for the truth, and took part in the Second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople in 381.

A theologian of great depth, he wrote profoundly on the Holy Trinity, the creation of man, and the soul's endless ascent toward God. He is commemorated on January 10.

1-11.name: Theodosius the Cenobiarch
1-11.desc: Founder of communal monastic life in Palestine.
1-11.bio:
St. Theodosius the Cenobiarch was born in Cappadocia in the fifth century and came as a young man to the Holy Land, where he embraced the ascetic life. Near Bethlehem he founded a great monastery of the common life, and he was appointed head of all the cenobitic monks of Palestine, whence his title Cenobiarch.

His monastery cared for the sick, the aged, and the poor, joining prayer to works of mercy, and he stood firm for the Orthodox faith in the disputes of his age. He reposed at a great age and is commemorated on January 11.

1-12.name: Tatiana
1-12.bio:
St. Tatiana was a deaconess of the Church of Rome who suffered martyrdom in the third century. Raised in a devout home, she served the Church in prayer and in care for the sick and the poor. Arrested in a time of persecution, she confessed Christ with courage and endured many tortures without denying her Lord.

Her steadfastness moved even some of her tormentors toward the faith, according to tradition. Beloved especially in Russia, where her name is widely given, she is commemorated on January 12.

1-13.name: Hermylos
1-13.bio:
St. Hermylos was a deacon who suffered for Christ under the Emperor Licinius in the early fourth century, in the region of Singidunum, the city known today as Belgrade. Refusing to deny his Lord, he was tortured and finally drowned in the waters of the Danube, together with his friend the jailer Stratonikos, who confessed Christ after witnessing his endurance.

The two friends, deacon and jailer, received the crown of martyrdom together. They are commemorated on January 13.

1-14.name: Nina
1-14.bio:
St. Nina, Equal-to-the-Apostles, was a young woman of Cappadocia who in the fourth century brought the Gospel to the land of Georgia. Traveling there alone, she lived in simplicity and prayer, carrying a cross woven of vine branches, and through her preaching and her healings the king and queen came to believe, and the whole nation received holy baptism.

Georgia honors her as its enlightener and mother in the faith, and her vine cross remains the emblem of the Georgian Church. She is commemorated on January 14.

1-15.name: Paul of Thebes
1-15.desc: The first Christian hermit saint in Egypt.
1-15.bio:
St. Paul of Thebes is honored as the first Christian hermit. Fleeing the persecution of Decius in the third century, he withdrew into the inner desert of Egypt, where he lived unknown to the world for many decades in fasting, solitude, and unceasing prayer.

Near the end of his long life he was found by St. Anthony the Great, who was sent to him by God and later buried him, and through Anthony his hidden life was made known to the Church. He is commemorated on January 15.

1-16.name: Peter
1-16.desc: Veneration of the chains of St. Peter.
1-16.bio:
On this day the Church venerates the precious chains of the holy Apostle Peter. The Acts of the Apostles relates how Peter, imprisoned by Herod and bound in chains, was freed in the night by an angel of the Lord, the chains falling from his hands as he was led out past the sleeping guards.

The faithful preserved these chains with reverence, and many blessings were received by those who venerated them with faith. The feast honors the chief apostle and the power of God who looses every bond. It is kept on January 16.

1-17.name: Anthony the Great
1-17.desc: Father of all monks and hermits.
1-17.bio:
St. Anthony the Great, the father of monasticism, was born in Egypt in the middle of the third century. Hearing in church the Gospel call to sell all, give to the poor, and follow Christ, he gave away his inheritance and withdrew into the desert, where he spent the rest of his long life in prayer, labor, and fierce spiritual struggle.

His holiness drew multitudes, and the desert became a city of monks who took him as their guide. His life, written by St. Athanasios of Alexandria, spread monasticism throughout the Christian world. He reposed at a great age around the year 356, and is commemorated on January 17.

1-18.name: Athanasios of Athos
1-18.desc: Founder of the Great Lavra monastery on Mount Athos.
1-18.bio:
St. Athanasios the Athonite was a monk of the tenth century who founded the Great Lavra, the first and foremost of the great monasteries of Mount Athos. Trained in learning in Constantinople, he fled honors for the ascetic life, and on the Holy Mountain he gathered the hermits into an ordered brotherhood, laboring with his own hands to build the monastery.

He is honored as a father of Athonite monasticism, whose Lavra still stands after a thousand years. In this calendar his memory is kept on January 18, the great name day of all who bear the name Athanasios.

1-19.name: Makarios of Egypt
1-19.desc: Desert father and abbot of the Egyptian monks.
1-19.bio:
St. Makarios of Egypt, called the Great, was one of the foremost of the desert fathers of the fourth century. Retiring to the desert of Scetis, he became the father of the monks who gathered there, renowned for his humility, his gentleness toward sinners, and his deep experience of prayer.

Many of his sayings are preserved among the words of the desert fathers, and spiritual homilies handed down under his name have nourished the Church for centuries. He reposed at a great age and is commemorated on January 19.

1-20.name: Euthymios the Great
1-20.desc: Great monastic father of the Palestinian desert.
1-20.bio:
St. Euthymios the Great was born in Melitene of Armenia in the fourth century and became one of the great fathers of the Palestinian desert. Settling in the wilderness east of Jerusalem, he founded a famous lavra, guided multitudes of monks, and formed disciples who themselves became pillars of monasticism, among them St. Savas the Sanctified.

A staunch defender of the Orthodox faith of the Council of Chalcedon, he reposed at a very great age in the fifth century. He is commemorated on January 20.

1-21.name: Maximos the Confessor
1-21.desc: Theologian and confessor who defended Orthodoxy.
1-21.bio:
St. Maximos the Confessor was a monk and theologian of the seventh century. Leaving high office in Constantinople for the monastic life, he became the great champion of the truth that Christ, being true God and true man, possesses both a divine and a human will, standing almost alone against the Monothelite heresy supported by emperor and patriarch.

For his confession he was tried, mutilated, and exiled, dying in banishment; the Church soon vindicated his teaching. His profound writings on the spiritual life are treasured to this day. He is commemorated on January 21.

1-22.name: Timothy the Apostle
1-22.desc: Holy Apostle Timothy, disciple of Paul.
1-22.bio:
St. Timothy the Apostle was the beloved disciple and fellow worker of St. Paul, who called him his true child in the faith. A native of Lystra, born of a Greek father and a devout Jewish mother, he accompanied Paul on his journeys and received from him the two epistles that bear his name. He served as the first Bishop of Ephesus.

According to tradition he ended his life as a martyr in Ephesus, struck down by pagans whose idolatrous festival he had rebuked. He is commemorated on January 22.

1-23.name: Clement of Ankyra
1-23.bio:
St. Clement was Bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, in Asia Minor, during the great persecutions at the turn of the fourth century. Tradition relates that he endured an extraordinarily long martyrdom, suffering imprisonments and tortures over many years in city after city, yet never wavering in his confession of Christ.

With him is honored the martyr Agathangelos, who shared his bonds and his sufferings. Clement finished his course by the sword, receiving the crown he had so long awaited. They are commemorated on January 23.

1-24.name: Xenia of Petersburg
1-24.desc: Blessed Xenia of St. Petersburg, fool-for-Christ.
1-24.bio:
Blessed Xenia of St. Petersburg lived in the eighteenth century. Widowed at twenty-six when her husband died suddenly, she gave away her possessions, put on his military coat, and took up the ascetic path of the fool-for-Christ, wandering the streets of the city for some forty-five years, praying at night in the fields and secretly helping the poor.

The people came to revere her as a woman of God, and her prayers were sought for healing, for families, and for those in need. She is invoked especially for help in finding work, housing, and a spouse. The Church commemorates her on January 24.

1-25.name: Gregory the Theologian
1-25.desc: Archbishop of Constantinople, one of the Three Holy Hierarchs.
1-25.bio:
St. Gregory the Theologian was born in Cappadocia in the fourth century and studied in Athens with his close friend St. Basil the Great. A man of deep prayer and unmatched eloquence, he was called to Constantinople when the city was dominated by Arianism, and through his celebrated theological orations restored the Orthodox faith in the Holy Trinity. He briefly served as Archbishop of Constantinople before withdrawing to a life of quiet and asceticism.

The Church has given the title Theologian only to him, to St. John the Evangelist, and to St. Symeon the New Theologian. One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, he is commemorated on January 25.

1-26.name: Xenophon
1-26.desc: Venerable Xenophon and Mary of Constantinople.
1-26.bio:
St. Xenophon was a devout and wealthy man of Constantinople in the sixth century, who with his wife Mary raised their two sons, Arkadios and John, in the fear of God. When the young men were shipwrecked on a voyage to their studies, each was saved without the other's knowledge, and each in gratitude took up the monastic life in the Holy Land.

Seeking their sons, Xenophon and Mary found them by God's providence, and the whole family gave itself to Christ in monasticism. They are commemorated together on January 26.

1-27.name: John Chrysostom
1-27.bio:
St. John Chrysostom, the Golden-Mouthed, was born in Antioch in the fourth century. First a monk and then a priest famed for his preaching, he was taken to Constantinople and consecrated its Archbishop. He preached constantly on the Scriptures, gave generously to the poor, and fearlessly rebuked the luxury and injustice of the powerful, for which he was twice driven into exile, dying with words of thanksgiving, glorifying God for all things.

The Divine Liturgy most often served in the Orthodox Church bears his name. One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, he is commemorated on January 27, the return of his relics to Constantinople, and again on November 13.

1-28.name: Ephrem the Syrian
1-28.desc: Poet, theologian and hymn-writer of the Syrian church.
1-28.bio:
St. Ephrem the Syrian was born in Nisibis in Mesopotamia early in the fourth century and later settled in Edessa. A deacon who out of humility refused higher office, he became the greatest hymnographer of the Syriac church, called the Harp of the Holy Spirit, and his hymns and homilies taught the faith to generations.

A man of deep compunction, he wrote constantly of repentance, and the Lenten prayer that bears his name is offered throughout the Great Fast in every Orthodox church. He reposed in 373 and is commemorated on January 28.

1-29.name: Ignatios the God-Bearer
1-29.desc: Bishop of Antioch and apostolic father.
1-29.bio:
St. Ignatios the God-Bearer was Bishop of Antioch and one of the apostolic fathers, a disciple of the apostles themselves. Condemned under the Emperor Trajan at the beginning of the second century, he was taken in bonds to Rome and given to the wild beasts in the arena, going to his death with joy, longing, as he wrote, to be ground as the wheat of God.

The seven epistles he wrote on that final journey remain treasures of the early Church. On January 29 the Church commemorates the translation of his relics; his martyrdom is kept on December 20.

1-30.name: Hippolytos
1-30.bio:
St. Hippolytos was a martyr of the Church of Rome who gave his life for Christ during the persecutions of the third century. The synaxaria preserve little of his story beyond his faithful confession and his death for the Lord, in company with other martyrs of that city.

His memory has been kept from ancient times among the witnesses of the Roman Church, whose blood became the seed of the faith. He is commemorated on January 30.

1-30.name: Three Holy Hierarchs
1-30.desc: Feast of Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom.
1-30.bio:
The feast of the Three Holy Hierarchs honors together Sts. Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom, the great fathers and ecumenical teachers of the Church. According to tradition, the common feast was established in the eleventh century after disputes arose in Constantinople over which of the three was greatest; the hierarchs made known in a vision that they are one before God, and a shared commemoration was appointed.

Together they represent the harmony of theology, eloquence, and pastoral care. In Greece the day is also kept as the feast of education and letters, the patronal celebration of schools, teachers, and students.

1-31.name: Cyrus and John
1-31.bio:
Sts. Cyrus and John are honored among the Holy Unmercenaries, physicians who healed in the name of Christ without accepting payment. Cyrus was a physician of Alexandria and John a soldier who joined him; together they served the sick and strengthened the persecuted during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century.

Hastening to encourage a Christian woman and her daughters under arrest, they were themselves seized, confessed Christ, and were beheaded. The faithful have long sought their intercession for healing. They are commemorated on January 31.

2-1.name: Tryphon
2-1.bio:
St. Tryphon was born in the village of Campsada in Phrygia, in Asia Minor, where as a youth he tended geese. Endowed by God with grace to heal the sick and drive out evil spirits, he became known far beyond his village. During the persecution of Decius in the third century he confessed Christ, endured torture, and was condemned to death, receiving the martyr's crown while still young.

The faithful invoke him as a protector of gardens, fields, and vineyards, and his blessing is asked over crops against every pest. He is commemorated on February 1.

2-2.name: Presentation of the Lord
2-2.desc: Meeting of Our Lord Jesus Christ in the Temple — 40 days after Nativity.
2-2.bio:
Forty days after His Nativity, the infant Christ was brought to the Temple in Jerusalem by the Theotokos and the righteous Joseph, in fulfillment of the Law of Moses. There He was received into the arms of the Elder Simeon, to whom it had been revealed that he would not die before seeing the Messiah, and Simeon blessed God with the prayer now sung at every Vespers. The aged Prophetess Anna likewise gave thanks and spoke of the Child to all who awaited redemption.

This Great Feast, called in Greek the Ypapanti, the Meeting, celebrates the encounter of the Old Covenant with the New, and is kept on February 2.

2-3.name: Simeon the God-Receiver
2-3.desc: The Elder Simeon who received the infant Christ in the Temple.
2-3.bio:
The righteous Simeon the God-Receiver was the elder to whom it was revealed by the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he had seen the Christ of the Lord. When the infant Jesus was brought to the Temple forty days after His birth, Simeon received Him into his arms and blessed God with the prayer sung at every Vespers: Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace.

He is honored on the day after the feast of the Meeting of the Lord, together with the Prophetess Anna who also bore witness to the Child. His memory is kept on February 3.

2-4.name: Isidore of Pelusium
2-4.bio:
St. Isidore of Pelusium was an ascetic of Egypt in the fifth century, who lived in monastic retirement near the city of Pelusium at the mouth of the Nile. A man of wide learning and deep devotion to the Holy Scriptures, he revered the teaching of St. John Chrysostom and followed his example of bold and clear instruction.

He is remembered above all for his letters, written by the thousands to people of every rank, expounding the Scriptures and correcting faults with wisdom and charity. He is commemorated on February 4.

2-5.name: Agatha
2-5.bio:
St. Agatha was a virgin martyr of Sicily who suffered for Christ during the persecution of Decius in the third century. Of noble birth, she consecrated herself to the Lord, and when she refused the advances of the pagan governor she was subjected to cruel tortures, which she endured with unshaken faith, dying in prison from her sufferings.

She is greatly venerated in Sicily, above all in Catania, whose people have long sought her protection, and her name is honored throughout the Church, East and West. Her feast is kept on February 5.

2-6.name: Bukolos of Smyrna
2-6.desc: Bishop of Smyrna and disciple of John the Theologian.
2-6.bio:
St. Bukolos was a disciple of St. John the Theologian, who consecrated him the first Bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor. In the earliest days of the Church he shepherded his flock amid the surrounding paganism with gentleness and wisdom, bringing many to the faith of Christ.

Before his peaceful repose he consecrated as his successor St. Polycarp, the future hieromartyr, thus handing on the apostolic faith he had received from the Beloved Disciple. He is commemorated on February 6.

2-7.name: Parthenius
2-7.bio:
St. Parthenius was Bishop of Lampsakos, on the Hellespont in Asia Minor, in the fourth century, in the days of St. Constantine the Great. The son of a deacon, he was a simple fisherman in his youth, giving to the poor what he earned, and after his consecration he labored to turn his region from idolatry to Christ.

He was renowned as a wonderworker, healing the sick and delivering the afflicted through his prayers, and he reposed in peace. He is commemorated on February 7.

2-8.name: Theodore Stratelates
2-8.desc: Great Martyr Theodore Stratelates the Commander.
2-8.bio:
St. Theodore Stratelates, the Commander, was a general in the Roman army, admired for his bravery and his noble bearing. A Christian, he openly confessed Christ before the Emperor Licinius during the persecutions of the early fourth century, and for this he was subjected to cruel tortures and finally beheaded at Heraclea.

He is honored as a Great Martyr and, together with St. Theodore the Recruit, is one of the most beloved warrior saints of the Church, a patron of soldiers. He is commemorated on February 8.

2-9.name: Nicephorus
2-9.bio:
St. Nicephorus was a Christian of Antioch in the third century, remembered for a martyrdom born of humility. He had quarreled with a priest named Sapricius, and though Nicephorus repeatedly sought forgiveness, the priest refused to be reconciled. When persecution came, Sapricius was led to execution as a confessor, yet, devoid of love, he denied Christ at the last moment.

Nicephorus, who had begged his forgiveness even on the road, then confessed Christ himself and was beheaded, receiving the crown the unforgiving priest had lost. His story teaches that martyrdom without love profits nothing. He is commemorated on February 9.

2-10.name: Charalambos
2-10.desc: Holy Martyr Charalambos of Magnesia, patron against illness.
2-10.bio:
St. Charalambos was a priest of Magnesia in Asia Minor who suffered martyrdom in extreme old age, according to tradition at the age of 113, during the persecutions of the early third century. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, he endured torture with such serenity that many who witnessed his suffering came to believe in Christ.

He is among the most beloved saints of Greece, where countless churches bear his name. The faithful have long invoked him as a protector against sickness and plague, and as a guardian of flocks and fields. His feast is celebrated on February 10.

2-11.name: Blaise
2-11.bio:
St. Blaise was Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, a physician of both bodies and souls. During the persecutions of the early fourth century he was seized, and after enduring tortures for his confession of Christ he was beheaded. Tradition tells of his kindness even to wild beasts, and of a boy saved from choking through his prayer.

For this the faithful have long invoked him for ailments of the throat, and his veneration spread widely in both East and West. He is commemorated on February 11.

2-12.name: Meletios of Antioch
2-12.desc: Archbishop of Antioch, champion of Orthodoxy.
2-12.bio:
St. Meletios was Archbishop of Antioch in the fourth century, a gentle and steadfast champion of the Nicene faith. For his defense of the divinity of Christ against the Arians he was driven from his see into exile more than once, yet he never ceased to shepherd his flock in patience and peace.

Restored at last, he presided at the opening of the Second Ecumenical Council in Constantinople in 381, and reposed in the Lord while the council was in session, mourned by the whole Church. He is commemorated on February 12.

2-13.name: Martinian
2-13.desc: Venerable Martinian the Hermit of Caesarea.
2-13.bio:
St. Martinian was a hermit of the region of Caesarea in Palestine, who took up the ascetic life as a young man and dwelt for many years in the desert in prayer and fasting. Tradition tells of the fierce struggles he endured against temptation, and of the lengths to which he went to preserve his purity, fleeing at last to a bare rock in the sea and then wandering from place to place with no home but Christ.

He ended his days in peace, an example of vigilance and repentance. He is commemorated on February 13.

2-14.name: Auxentios
2-14.bio:
St. Auxentios lived in the fifth century and served for a time at the imperial court in Constantinople before forsaking the world for the life of a hermit. He settled on a mountain in Bithynia, not far from Chalcedon, where he lived in a small cell in fasting and prayer, receiving the many who climbed to him for counsel and healing.

He upheld the Orthodox faith of the Council of Chalcedon and was revered as a discerning elder and wonderworker. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on February 14.

2-15.name: Onesimos
2-15.desc: Holy Apostle Onesimos, disciple of Paul.
2-15.bio:
St. Onesimos the Apostle was the slave of Philemon of Colossae who fled from his master and, by God's providence, came to St. Paul in his imprisonment. There he was converted, and Paul sent him back with the Epistle to Philemon, asking that he be received no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother in Christ.

Numbered among the Seventy Apostles, he later served the Church in the preaching of the Gospel, and according to tradition he ended his life as a martyr. He is commemorated on February 15.

2-16.name: Pamphilos
2-16.bio:
St. Pamphilos was a priest of Caesarea in Palestine, a man of great learning who devoted his life to the study and careful copying of the Holy Scriptures and gathered a famous library for the Church. During the persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century he was imprisoned for his confession of Christ, and after a long captivity he was put to death together with a company of fellow martyrs.

The historian Eusebius, who loved him as a friend and teacher, preserved his memory for the whole Church. He is commemorated on February 16.

2-17.name: Theodore of Tyre
2-17.bio:
St. Theodore the Recruit, called Teron, was a young soldier in Asia Minor during the persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, he boldly confessed Christ, and after imprisonment and torture he was given over to death by fire, sealing his faith as a Great Martyr.

The Church also remembers his help after death: through him the faithful were warned to keep from food defiled by idols, and in his memory kolyva is blessed on the first Saturday of Great Lent. His feast is kept on February 17.

2-18.name: Leo the Great
2-18.desc: Pope Leo the Great of Rome.
2-18.bio:
St. Leo the Great was Pope of Rome in the fifth century, one of the great fathers of the undivided Church. His celebrated Tome, read at the Fourth Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon in 451, confessed with clarity that Christ is one Person in two natures, true God and true man, and the fathers of the council received it as the voice of Peter.

He shepherded Rome through perilous times, and tradition tells that he turned Attila the Hun away from the city. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on February 18.

2-19.name: Archippos
2-19.bio:
St. Archippos the Apostle is named in the New Testament, where St. Paul calls him his fellow soldier and bids him fulfill the ministry he received in the Lord. Numbered among the Seventy Apostles, he served the church at Colossae in the household of Philemon in the earliest days of the faith.

According to tradition he sealed his ministry with martyrdom, suffering for Christ in the time of the persecutions. He is commemorated on February 19.

2-20.name: Leo of Catania
2-20.bio:
St. Leo was Bishop of Catania in Sicily in the eighth century, a shepherd remembered for his mercy toward the poor and the sick, and honored as a wonderworker for the healings granted through his prayers. Tradition also tells of his boldness in confronting a notorious sorcerer who was leading the people astray, whose deceptions collapsed before the bishop's faith.

He reposed in peace, and his relics were venerated in his city. He is commemorated on February 20.

2-21.name: Timothy of Symbola
2-21.bio:
St. Timothy of Symbola was a monk who lived the ascetic life at the monastery of Symbola in Bithynia, in Asia Minor. From his youth he embraced obedience, fasting, and unceasing prayer, and the synaxaria remember him as a vessel of purity who received from God grace to heal the sick and drive away evil spirits.

Having lived to old age in holiness, he reposed in peace. He is commemorated on February 21.

2-23.name: Polykarpos
2-23.desc: Bishop of Smyrna, disciple of John the Theologian.
2-23.bio:
St. Polycarp was Bishop of Smyrna and a disciple of St. John the Theologian, a living link between the apostles and the generations that followed. He shepherded his church for many decades, and in extreme old age was arrested during a persecution in the second century. Urged to deny Christ, he answered that in eighty-six years the Lord had done him no wrong, and he could not blaspheme his King.

He was burned at the stake, and the account of his martyrdom, written by his church, is among the treasures of early Christianity. He is commemorated on February 23.

2-25.name: Tarasios
2-25.bio:
St. Tarasios was Patriarch of Constantinople at the end of the eighth century. A layman of high imperial office renowned for learning and virtue, he was raised to the patriarchal throne at a time when the Church was torn by the iconoclast heresy, and he accepted on the condition that the veneration of the holy icons be restored.

He presided over the Seventh Ecumenical Council at Nicaea in 787, which vindicated the icons, and he shepherded the Church with charity toward the poor until his peaceful repose. He is commemorated on February 25.

2-26.name: Porphyrios
2-26.bio:
St. Porphyrios was Bishop of Gaza at the turn of the fifth century. Born in Thessalonica, he lived as an ascetic in Egypt and the Holy Land before being called, against his desire, to the episcopate of Gaza, a city then still devoted to idols.

With patience and courage he labored to turn the city to Christ, obtaining the closing of its pagan temples and raising a great church in their place, while caring tenderly for the poor. He reposed in peace after many years of toil. He is commemorated on February 26.

2-27.name: Prokopios Dekapolis
2-27.bio:
St. Prokopios of the Dekapolis was a monk of the eighth century who lived the ascetic life in fasting, vigil, and prayer. When the iconoclast heresy arose under the emperors who warred against the holy images, he stood forth as a confessor, defending the veneration of the icons of Christ and His saints, and suffering persecution for the truth.

Having endured to the end, he reposed in peace, honored by the Church among the confessors of Orthodoxy. He is commemorated on February 27.

3-1.name: Eudokia
3-1.bio:
St. Eudokia was a Samaritan of Heliopolis in Phoenicia who lived in the early centuries of the Church. Wealthy and famed for her beauty, she was moved to repentance by the words of a monk named Germanos, was baptized, gave her riches to the poor, and entered the monastic life, excelling in fasting and prayer.

Tradition relates that she endured slander and persecution with patience, and at last completed her course as a martyr, beheaded for her confession of Christ. Honored as a model of repentance at the threshold of spring, she is commemorated on March 1.

3-3.name: Hesychios
3-3.bio:
St. Hesychios was a martyr of Antioch who suffered during the Roman persecutions of the early fourth century. Tradition remembers him as a man of rank who, when the emperor demanded that Christians in imperial service deny their faith or lose their honors, laid aside his dignities rather than deny Christ, and was put to death for his confession.

The synaxaria preserve little else of his life, but his choice of Christ over every earthly honor has kept his memory alive in the Church. He is commemorated on March 3.

3-4.name: Gerasimos of the Jordan
3-4.desc: Venerable Gerasimos of the Jordan who tamed a lion.
3-4.bio:
St. Gerasimos was a fifth-century ascetic who founded a great monastery in the desert by the River Jordan, guiding many monks in a strict rule of poverty, silence, and prayer, and was counted among the great elders of the Palestinian desert.

He is best remembered for the lion who, according to tradition, was healed by the saint of a thorn in its paw and thereafter served him tamely until his death — an image of paradise restored around a man of God. The Church commemorates him on March 4.

3-5.name: Konon
3-5.bio:
St. Konon was an early martyr from Isauria in Asia Minor, remembered as a man of simple and holy life who drew many of his countrymen from idolatry to faith in Christ. When persecution reached his homeland, he confessed the Lord openly and endured torture at the hands of the pagans.

The faithful of Isauria honored him from ancient times as a wonderworker and intercessor, and his veneration spread through the Christian East. He is commemorated on March 5.

3-5.name: Savas the Sanctified
3-5.desc: Founder of the Great Lavra monastery in Palestine.
3-5.bio:
St. Savas the Sanctified was born in Cappadocia in the fifth century and came as a young man to the Judean desert, where he became a disciple of the great elders of Palestine. In the wild gorge of the Kidron he founded the Great Lavra, which still bears his name, and became the leader and lawgiver of the monks of the desert.

His order of services deeply shaped the worship of the whole Orthodox Church, and his monastery has remained a fountain of holiness for fifteen centuries. He reposed at a great age and is commemorated on March 5.

3-6.name: Forty-Two Martyrs of Amorium
3-6.desc: The Forty-Two Holy Martyrs of Amorium.
3-6.bio:
The Forty-Two Martyrs of Amorium were Byzantine officers taken captive when the city of Amorium in Asia Minor fell to the Arabs in the year 838. Held in harsh imprisonment for some seven years, they were pressed again and again to abandon Christ and accept the faith of their captors, with freedom and honors promised if they yielded.

Every one of them refused, and they were beheaded together by the river Euphrates in 845. The Church honors their long, unbroken confession, sealed after years of suffering, and commemorates them on March 6.

3-2.name: Efthalia
3-2.bio:
St. Efthalia was a virgin martyr of Sicily in the early centuries of the Church. Tradition relates that she came to faith in Christ together with her mother, and that when her pagan brother raged against her confession she would not renounce the Lord, and so gave her life for the faith.

The synaxaria preserve little else of her story, but the Church has kept her memory as one of the pure virgin martyrs whose steadfastness shone within her own household. She is commemorated on March 2.

3-22.name: Basil of Ancyra
3-22.bio:
St. Basil was a priest of the church of Ancyra in Asia Minor in the fourth century. A faithful shepherd who strengthened his flock against both paganism and heresy, he was seized during the reign of Julian the Apostate, when the emperor sought to restore the worship of idols. Refusing to deny Christ, he endured cruel tortures and completed his course as a martyr around the year 362.

His fearless answers before his persecutors are preserved in the tradition of the Church, which honors him as a model of priestly courage. He is commemorated on March 22.

3-23.name: Nikon
3-23.desc: Holy Martyr Nikon of Sicily and his 199 disciples.
3-23.bio:
St. Nikon lived in the third century. A soldier's son who came to faith in Christ, he was baptized, embraced the monastic life, and was later made a bishop, gathering many disciples whom he guided in prayer and asceticism. Fleeing persecution, he settled with them in Sicily.

There, during the persecutions of that age, he was seized together with one hundred ninety-nine of his disciples, and all of them were put to death for their confession of Christ, the shepherd suffering last of all. The Church commemorates St. Nikon and his disciples on March 23.

3-8.name: Zacharias
3-8.desc: Prophet Zacharias, father of John the Baptist.
3-8.bio:
The holy Prophet Zacharias was a priest of the Temple in Jerusalem and the father of St. John the Forerunner. As the Gospel of Luke relates, the Archangel Gabriel appeared to him at the altar of incense and announced that his aged wife Elizabeth would bear a son; when John was born, Zacharias was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied of the dawn from on high.

Tradition honors him as both prophet and martyr, holding that he was slain in the Temple for his faithfulness to God. He is commemorated on March 8.

3-9.name: Forty Holy Martyrs of Sebaste
3-9.desc: The Forty Holy Martyrs who froze in the lake of Sebaste.
3-9.bio:
The Forty Holy Martyrs of Sebaste were Roman soldiers who confessed Christ in Armenia in the year 320, during the persecution of Licinius. Refusing to deny the Lord, they were condemned to stand through the night upon a frozen lake, with warm baths set on the shore to tempt them. One gave way, but a guard, beholding crowns descending upon the martyrs, confessed Christ and took his place, completing the forty.

Their memory on March 9 is kept with love in the midst of the Great Fast, honored as an image of endurance to the end. In Greek tradition the day is the name day of Sarantis.

3-10.name: Anastasios the Confessor
3-10.bio:
St. Anastasios was a hierarch of the Church of Jerusalem who bore the title of confessor, one who suffered for the faith without denying Christ. The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond his faithful witness in a time when the Church was tried by heresy and persecution.

The Church honors in him the countless shepherds who guarded the flock of Christ at cost to themselves, their names written more fully in heaven than in the records of men. He is commemorated on March 10.

3-11.name: Sophronios of Jerusalem
3-11.bio:
St. Sophronios, Patriarch of Jerusalem, was born in Damascus in the sixth century. A monk and a learned theologian, he traveled the monasteries of the East with his friend John Moschos, and as patriarch he stood firm against the Monothelite heresy, defending the fullness of both the divine and human wills in Christ.

It fell to him to shepherd the Holy City in its darkest hour, when Jerusalem passed under Arab rule in his old age, and he labored to protect his flock and the holy places. A hymnographer of great beauty, he is commemorated on March 11.

3-12.name: Theophanes the Confessor
3-12.bio:
St. Theophanes the Confessor was born in Constantinople in the eighth century to a noble family. Renouncing wealth and worldly marriage, he embraced the monastic life and founded a monastery, where he became famed for asceticism and learning; his great chronicle of world history earned him the title Chronographer.

When the iconoclast persecution was renewed, he refused to reject the holy icons, and though aged and ill he was imprisoned and exiled, dying a confessor for the veneration of the icons. He is commemorated on March 12.

3-13.name: Nikephoros of Constantinople
3-13.bio:
St. Nikephoros was Patriarch of Constantinople in the early ninth century, during the second wave of iconoclasm. A learned defender of the veneration of the holy icons, he stood against the emperor Leo the Armenian, and for his faithfulness he was deposed from his throne and driven into exile, where he spent his remaining years in prayer and writing until his repose.

After the final triumph of Orthodoxy his relics were returned in honor to Constantinople, an event the Church remembers with joy. He is commemorated on March 13.

3-14.name: Benedict of Nursia
3-14.bio:
St. Benedict was born in Nursia in Italy in the late fifth century. Leaving his studies in Rome to flee the corruption of the world, he lived first as a hermit in a cave at Subiaco, and later founded the great monastery of Monte Cassino. His Rule for monks, marked by prayer, labor, moderation, and obedience, shaped the whole monastic life of the Christian West.

Revered as the father of Western monasticism, he reposed in the sixth century and is honored throughout the Church, East and West alike. He is commemorated on March 14.

3-15.name: Agapios
3-15.bio:
St. Agapios was a martyr who suffered at Caesarea in Palestine during the great persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century. Together with several companions, he confessed Christ before the governor and refused every inducement to sacrifice to the idols, and so was put to death for the faith.

His name, which means beloved, befits one who loved Christ more than life itself. The Church commemorates St. Agapios and his fellow martyrs on March 15.

3-17.name: Alexios Man of God
3-17.bio:
St. Alexios, the Man of God, was the son of a noble Roman family. On the night of his wedding he secretly left his home, choosing poverty for the sake of Christ, and lived for years as a beggar in the East, spending his days in fasting and prayer at the doors of the church.

Tradition relates that he returned at last to his father's house, where he lived unrecognized as a poor stranger, enduring contempt with patience; only at his death was it revealed who he was. A beloved image of hidden holiness, he is commemorated on March 17.

3-18.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
3-18.desc: Archbishop of Jerusalem and great catechist.
3-18.bio:
St. Cyril was Archbishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century, a gentle and learned shepherd of the Holy City. His famous Catechetical Lectures, delivered to those preparing for baptism, remain one of the treasures of the ancient Church, setting forth the faith and the holy mysteries with clarity and warmth.

For his defense of the Orthodox faith against Arianism he was driven from his throne several times, spending years in exile before being restored. He reposed in peace near the end of the fourth century and is commemorated on March 18.

3-19.name: Chrysanthos and Daria
3-19.bio:
Sts. Chrysanthos and Daria were martyrs of Rome in the third century. Chrysanthos, the son of a pagan noble, came to faith in Christ through the reading of the Scriptures; when his father arranged his marriage to Daria, a learned pagan woman, Chrysanthos won her to the faith, and the two lived in purity, devoting themselves to prayer and to bringing others to Christ.

Denounced as Christians, they endured tortures and were put to death together for their confession. The Church commemorates this holy pair on March 19.

3-20.name: Mother of God of Iveron
3-20.desc: Feast of the Iveron Icon of the Theotokos.
3-20.bio:
The Iveron Icon of the Theotokos, the Portaitissa or Gate-Keeper, is one of the most venerated icons of the Mother of God. According to tradition, during the iconoclast persecutions a pious widow entrusted the icon to the sea; generations later it appeared in a pillar of light off Mount Athos and was received by the monks of the Iveron Monastery, where it has remained for a thousand years as protectress of the Holy Mountain.

Many miracles are ascribed to the Portaitissa, and copies of the icon are venerated throughout the Orthodox world. The Church commemorates the icon on this day with thanksgiving to the Theotokos.

3-21.name: Thomas the Apostle
3-21.bio:
St. Thomas, called the Twin, was one of the Twelve Apostles of the Lord. It was he who said he would not believe unless he touched the wounds of the risen Christ, and who, beholding the Lord eight days after Pascha, made the great confession, my Lord and my God. His honest doubt became for all generations a confirmation of the Resurrection.

According to ancient tradition he carried the Gospel to the East, preaching as far as India, where he completed his apostolic labors as a martyr. He is commemorated on March 21.

3-25.name: Annunciation
3-25.desc: The Annunciation of the Most Holy Theotokos — Archangel Gabriel announces the Incarnation.
3-25.bio:
The Great Feast of the Annunciation commemorates the day the Archangel Gabriel was sent to the Virgin Mary in Nazareth to announce that she would conceive and bear the Son of God. Her humble acceptance as the handmaid of the Lord opened the way for the Incarnation, and at that moment the Word of God took flesh in her womb.

Celebrated on March 25, nine months before the Nativity of Christ, the Annunciation is one of the most beloved feasts of the Theotokos. For the Greek people the day carries a double joy, as it also marks the beginning of the struggle for independence in 1821.

4-1.name: Mary of Egypt
4-1.desc: Venerable Mary of Egypt, great penitent saint.
4-1.bio:
St. Mary of Egypt is the great example of repentance. Living in Alexandria in the fifth and sixth centuries, she spent her youth in sin; traveling to Jerusalem, she was held back from entering the Church of the Holy Sepulchre by an unseen power, and, praying before the icon of the Theotokos, she was converted. Crossing the Jordan, she lived some forty-seven years alone in the desert in fasting and prayer.

Near the end of her life she was found by the elder Zosimas, who heard her story and gave her Holy Communion. She is commemorated on April 1 and on the fifth Sunday of Great Lent.

4-4.name: Titos
4-4.desc: Holy Apostle Titus, disciple of Paul.
4-4.bio:
St. Titus was a disciple and companion of the Apostle Paul, who called him his true son in the common faith. A Greek by birth, he accompanied Paul on his apostolic journeys, was entrusted with delicate missions to the churches, and received the epistle that bears his name, in which Paul instructs him in the ordering of the Church.

According to tradition Paul established him as bishop of Crete, where he shepherded the faithful to a great old age and reposed in peace, the father of the Church of that island. He is commemorated on April 4.

4-4.name: Claudia
4-4.bio:
St. Claudia was a martyr of the early Church who suffered for Christ during the Roman persecutions. The synaxaria preserve little of her life beyond her faithful confession, numbering her among the holy women who chose death rather than deny the Lord.

In honoring her, the Church honors the great company of women martyrs whose names are known while their full stories are written in heaven. She is commemorated on April 4.

4-5.name: Theodoulos
4-5.bio:
St. Theodoulos was a young reader of the church of Thessaloniki who suffered martyrdom during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Tradition remembers him together with the elder deacon Agathopous; refusing to surrender the holy books or deny Christ, the two were condemned and cast into the sea.

The Church honors in him the courage of the young, who at the very start of life counted Christ dearer than all its promise. He is commemorated on April 5.

4-6.name: Eutychios
4-6.bio:
St. Eutychios was Patriarch of Constantinople in the sixth century, in the days of the emperor Justinian. A monk raised to the patriarchal throne, he presided at the Fifth Ecumenical Council, and later, refusing to accept a teaching that compromised the reality of Christ's human nature, he was deposed and spent years in exile in a monastery.

Restored at last to his throne, he ended his days in peace, honored as a confessor for the truth of the Incarnation. He is commemorated on April 6.

4-8.name: Kalliope
4-8.bio:
St. Kalliope is honored among the martyrs of the early Church, one of those who suffered for Christ during the Roman persecutions. The synaxaria preserve little of her life beyond her faithful confession unto death.

Her name, which in Greek means beautiful voice, has been borne by generations of faithful women in her honor, and the Church keeps her memory among the victorious martyrs. She is commemorated on April 8.

4-9.name: Eudemos
4-9.bio:
St. Eudemos is remembered among the martyrs of the early Church, one who confessed Christ in the time of the persecutions and sealed his faith with suffering. The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond this faithful witness.

The Church honors in him and in the countless martyrs like him the cloud of witnesses whose endurance watered the seed of the Gospel. He is commemorated on April 9.

4-10.name: Terence
4-10.bio:
St. Terence was a martyr of North Africa who suffered in the third century, during the persecution of the emperor Decius. Together with a company of fellow Christians, he confessed Christ before the proconsul, endured imprisonment and torments without wavering, and was beheaded with his companions.

The Church remembers this band of African martyrs as an image of brotherly steadfastness, many suffering as one body for the one Lord. St. Terence and his companions are commemorated on April 10.

4-11.name: Antipas of Pergamon
4-11.bio:
St. Antipas was Bishop of Pergamon in Asia Minor in the first century, a disciple of the Apostle John. He is named in the Book of Revelation, where the Lord Himself calls him my faithful witness, slain among you where Satan dwells. Tradition relates that he was put to death by the pagans of Pergamon for refusing to honor their idols.

From ancient times the faithful have sought his intercession, invoking him especially for relief from ailments of the teeth. He is commemorated on April 11.

4-12.name: Basil of Parion
4-12.bio:
St. Basil was Bishop of Parion in Asia Minor during the age of iconoclasm. Refusing to consent to the condemnation of the holy icons, he was driven from his see and spent long years in hardship and wandering, enduring persecution rather than betray the fullness of the faith.

The Church numbers him among the confessors whose sufferings preserved the veneration of the icons for the whole Orthodox world. He is commemorated on April 12.

4-13.name: Martin the Confessor
4-13.bio:
St. Martin the Confessor was Pope of Rome in the seventh century. He convened a council at the Lateran which condemned the Monothelite heresy, defending the fullness of Christ's humanity against the will of the emperor. For this he was seized by imperial soldiers, carried off to Constantinople, tried and mistreated, and exiled to Cherson on the Black Sea.

Worn down by hunger and hardship, he died in exile, a confessor for the Orthodox faith honored by East and West alike. He is commemorated on April 13.

4-17.name: Ariadne
4-17.bio:
St. Ariadne was a Christian servant in Phrygia in the early centuries of the Church. When she refused to take part in the pagan festivities of her master's household, she was punished for her faith and pursued when she fled. Tradition relates that as her persecutors closed upon her she prayed, and a rock opened to receive her, taking her beyond their reach into the hands of God.

The Church honors her as a martyr in will and deed, a lowly servant whose faithfulness shamed the powerful. She is commemorated on April 17.

4-19.name: John of the Ladder
4-19.desc: Abbot of Sinai and author of The Ladder of Divine Ascent.
4-19.bio:
St. John of the Ladder gave his whole life to Mount Sinai, entering the monastery there in his youth, living long years as a hermit in the desert nearby, and at last serving as abbot of the holy mountain of Moses. From the depths of his experience he wrote The Ladder of Divine Ascent, a guide of thirty steps by which the soul climbs from renunciation of the world to the summit of faith, hope, and love.

His book remains a cornerstone of Orthodox spiritual life, read aloud in monasteries each Great Lent. He is commemorated on April 19.

4-21.name: Anastasios of Antioch
4-21.bio:
St. Anastasios was Patriarch of Antioch in the sixth century, a theologian and ascetic who shepherded one of the great sees of the East in a turbulent age. Standing firm for the Orthodox teaching on the Incarnation against imperial pressure, he was driven from his throne and endured long years of exile before being restored to his flock.

The Church honors him among the confessor hierarchs who preferred banishment to the least compromise of the faith. He is commemorated on April 21.

4-22.name: Theodore Sykeon
4-22.bio:
St. Theodore of Sykeon was born in a village of Galatia in Asia Minor in the sixth century. Given to prayer and fasting from childhood, he became a monk of extraordinary asceticism, and his holiness drew crowds seeking healing and counsel; against his will he was made a bishop, though he later returned to his beloved monastic quiet.

Famed as a wonderworker in his own lifetime, he was sought out by emperors and peasants alike, and reposed early in the seventh century. He is commemorated on April 22.

4-23.name: George the Great Martyr
4-23.desc: Great Martyr George the Trophy-Bearer, patron of soldiers.
4-23.bio:
St. George the Great Martyr and Trophy-Bearer was a Roman officer from Cappadocia who suffered for Christ under the Emperor Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Confessing his faith openly before the emperor, he endured many tortures and was beheaded, and his courage brought many to belief.

One of the most venerated saints in both East and West, he is honored as patron of soldiers and invoked as a swift helper in danger. Tradition depicts him as the dragon-slayer, an image of faith triumphing over evil. His feast on April 23 is one of the great name days of the Greek world; when it falls before Pascha it is transferred to Bright Monday.

4-24.name: Elizabeth
4-24.bio:
St. Elizabeth was a holy woman of Constantinople who from her youth gave herself wholly to God in the monastic life. Excelling in fasting, vigil, and compassion for the poor, she became the spiritual mother of a community of nuns, and the faithful sought her prayers, through which many received healing.

Her memory has been kept in the Church from ancient times as an image of quiet, hidden sanctity bearing abundant fruit. She is commemorated on April 24.

4-24.name: Simeon Stylites the Younger
4-24.bio:
St. Simeon Stylites the Younger was born in Antioch in the sixth century. Drawn to asceticism from early childhood, he took up the extraordinary struggle of the pillar-dwellers, living for the greater part of his long life atop a column on the mountain near Antioch called the Wonderful Mountain, in unceasing prayer and fasting.

A priest and wonderworker, he counseled and healed the multitudes who climbed to him, and a monastery grew up around his pillar. He reposed in old age near the end of the sixth century, and is commemorated on April 24.

4-25.name: Mark the Evangelist
4-25.bio:
St. Mark the Evangelist, one of the Seventy, was a companion of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and wrote the second Gospel, which ancient tradition holds preserves the preaching of Peter. He labored in the spread of the Gospel from Jerusalem to Rome, and is honored as the founder of the Church of Alexandria in Egypt.

There, according to tradition, he was seized by the pagans and dragged through the streets, completing his apostolic course as a martyr. The father of one of the great ancient Churches, he is commemorated on April 25.

4-26.name: Basil of Amaseia
4-26.bio:
St. Basil was Bishop of Amaseia in Pontus in the early fourth century, in the last days of the persecutions. A fearless shepherd who protected those who fled to the Church for refuge, he drew upon himself the anger of the emperor Licinius, and was put to death for his faithfulness, his body cast into the sea.

Tradition relates that his relics were recovered by the faithful and buried with honor in his own city. The Church commemorates him on April 26.

5-1.name: Jeremiah the Prophet
5-1.bio:
The Holy Prophet Jeremiah lived in Jerusalem in the seventh and sixth centuries before Christ. Called by God from his youth, he warned the people of Judah of the coming destruction of the city for their unfaithfulness, and wept over its fall in his Lamentations. His words were often rejected, and he suffered imprisonment for speaking the truth; tradition holds that he ended his life in Egypt.

The Church honors him among the four great prophets, for his prophecies of the new covenant God would write upon the hearts of His people point to Christ. He is commemorated on May 1.

5-2.name: Athanasios of Alexandria
5-2.desc: Archbishop of Alexandria, defender of the Nicene faith.
5-2.bio:
St. Athanasios the Great was Archbishop of Alexandria in the fourth century and the foremost defender of the divinity of Christ against the Arian heresy. Present at the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea as a young deacon, he spent the rest of his life upholding the Nicene faith, enduring five exiles rather than yield.

His writings, including On the Incarnation and the Life of St. Anthony, shaped the faith and the monasticism of the whole Church. He reposed in 373. The Church commemorates him on January 18 together with St. Cyril, and on May 2 the return of his relics.

5-3.name: Timothy and Maura
5-3.desc: Holy Martyrs Timothy and Maura of Egypt.
5-3.bio:
The Holy Martyrs Timothy and Maura were a young Christian couple of Egypt who suffered during the persecution of Diocletian at the end of the third century. Timothy was a reader of the Church, entrusted with the sacred books; only days after their marriage the two were arrested when he refused to surrender them. Together they endured cruel tortures and were crucified, encouraging one another in the faith to the end.

Their witness is a treasured image of married love made perfect in Christ, two lives offered together rather than parted from the Lord. They are commemorated on May 3.

5-3.name: Peter of Argos
5-3.bio:
St. Peter, Bishop of Argos, was a monk of deep humility who lived in the ninth and tenth centuries. Long refusing episcopal office, he was at last persuaded to shepherd the Church of Argos in the Peloponnese, where he became a father to his flock, feeding the hungry in time of famine, ransoming captives, and caring for orphans and the poor.

He was revered even in his lifetime as a wonderworker, and after his repose his relics became a source of healing. He remains a beloved saint of the Peloponnese, commemorated on May 3.

5-4.name: Pelagia
5-4.bio:
The Holy Martyr Pelagia was a young Christian woman of the early Church who suffered during the persecutions of the pagan emperors. Refusing to deny Christ or to be turned from her purity, she gave her life rather than betray her Lord, and the synaxaria honor her steadfast confession.

Her name, which means 'of the sea', has been borne with love by generations of Orthodox women in her memory. She is commemorated on May 4.

5-5.name: Irene the Great Martyr
5-5.bio:
The Holy Great Martyr Irene lived in the early centuries of the Church. According to tradition she was the daughter of a pagan ruler and came to faith in Christ in her youth, receiving in baptism the name Irene, which means peace. Confessing the Lord openly, she endured many tortures with courage, and her endurance drew multitudes to belief.

She is honored as one of the great women martyrs of the Church, and many churches across the Greek world bear her name. Her feast on May 5 is the beloved name day of all who bear the name Irene.

5-6.name: Job the Long-Suffering
5-6.bio:
The Righteous Job lived in the land of Uz in the age of the patriarchs, a man blameless and upright who feared God and turned away from evil. Tested by the loss of his wealth, his children, and his health, he refused to curse God, saying that the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away, blessed be the name of the Lord.

His patience under affliction has comforted the suffering in every generation, and the Church reads his book in Holy Week, seeing in the righteous sufferer a foreshadowing of Christ. He is commemorated on May 6.

5-7.name: Akakios of Cappadocia
5-7.bio:
The Holy Martyr Akakios was a young soldier from Cappadocia who suffered for Christ at the beginning of the fourth century, during the persecutions of the pagan emperors. Denounced as a Christian, he confessed the Lord boldly before his commanders, endured imprisonment and torture without wavering, and was beheaded at Byzantium.

He was venerated there from early times, and a church was raised in his honor in the city that became Constantinople. His faithful confession is kept in memory by the Church on May 7.

5-8.name: John the Theologian
5-8.desc: Holy Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian, the Beloved Disciple.
5-8.bio:
St. John the Theologian, the Beloved Disciple, was the son of Zebedee and brother of James, called from his nets by the Lord. He leaned on the breast of Christ at the Mystical Supper, stood by the Cross when the others had fled, and received the Theotokos into his care. He wrote the Fourth Gospel, three Epistles, and the Revelation.

According to tradition he lived to a great age in Ephesus, teaching his disciples above all to love one another. One of the few saints the Church names Theologian, he is commemorated on May 8 and at his repose on September 26.

5-9.name: Isaiah the Prophet
5-9.bio:
The Holy Prophet Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem in the eighth century before Christ. Beholding the Lord upon His throne, with the seraphim crying Holy, Holy, Holy, he was cleansed by a burning coal and sent to call the people to repentance. His book is filled with prophecies of the Messiah, of the virgin who would conceive, and of the suffering servant wounded for our transgressions.

For the clarity of these prophecies he is called the evangelist among the prophets, and tradition holds that he died a martyr. He is commemorated on May 9.

5-10.name: Simon the Zealot
5-10.bio:
The Holy Apostle Simon the Zealot was one of the Twelve chosen by the Lord. The Gospels record his name among the Apostles, and his title of Zealot bespeaks his burning devotion. After Pentecost he went forth like the others to preach the Gospel, and tradition holds that he carried the good news to distant lands and completed his course as a martyr.

Though the synaxaria preserve few details of his labors, the Church honors him as one of the foundation stones of apostolic preaching. He is commemorated on May 10.

5-12.name: Modestos
5-12.bio:
The Holy Martyr Modestos suffered for Christ in the early centuries of the Church. Of his life the synaxaria preserve little beyond his faithful confession, that he refused to deny the Lord and sealed his witness with his blood.

The Church keeps his memory among the countless martyrs whose names are written in heaven, honoring in him the victory of faith over the fear of death. He is commemorated on May 12.

5-13.name: Glykeria
5-13.bio:
The Holy Martyr Glykeria was a young Christian woman of Thrace who suffered for Christ in the second century. The daughter of a Roman official, she confessed the Lord openly when the pagans of Heraclea gathered for sacrifice, refusing to honor the idols. For this she endured imprisonment and many tortures, and was finally given over to wild beasts, ending her contest with prayer.

Her name means sweetness, and the Church remembers in her the sweetness of a soul wholly given to Christ. She is commemorated on May 13.

5-14.name: Isidore of Chios
5-14.bio:
The Holy Martyr Isidore suffered on the island of Chios in the middle of the third century, during the persecution of Decius. A soldier serving in the imperial fleet, he was denounced as a Christian, and when he refused to sacrifice to the idols he was tortured and beheaded, remaining steadfast in his confession to the end.

He has been venerated on Chios from ancient times as the island's own martyr, and churches in his honor spread from there throughout the Christian world. He is commemorated on May 14.

5-15.name: Pachomios the Great
5-15.desc: Founder of communal monasticism in Egypt.
5-15.bio:
St. Pachomios the Great was born in Egypt at the end of the third century. A pagan conscript soldier, he was won to Christ by the kindness of Christians to the troops, and after baptism took up the ascetic life in the desert. At Tabennisi by the Nile he founded the first great communities of monks living a common life under a rule, and thousands gathered under his guidance.

With St. Anthony he stands at the head of Egyptian monasticism, the father of the cenobitic way that spread through the whole Church. He reposed in the fourth century and is commemorated on May 15.

5-16.name: Theodore the Sanctified
5-16.bio:
St. Theodore the Sanctified was the beloved disciple of St. Pachomios the Great in fourth-century Egypt. Coming to Tabennisi as a youth, he so gave himself to obedience and prayer that Pachomios loved him as a son, and after the death of his elder he guided the great communities of monks, healing divisions and strengthening the brotherhood in the common life.

He is called the Sanctified from the holiness of his life, and the Church honors him beside his teacher as a pillar of Egyptian monasticism. He is commemorated on May 16.

5-17.name: Andronikos the Apostle
5-17.bio:
The Holy Apostle Andronikos was one of the Seventy, greeted by St. Paul in the Epistle to the Romans as his kinsman and fellow prisoner, notable among the apostles and in Christ before him. With his fellow laborer Junia he preached the Gospel and turned many from idols to the living God.

Tradition honors him as a tireless missionary of the apostolic age whose labors bore fruit in many lands. He is commemorated on May 17.

5-21.name: Constantine and Helen
5-21.desc: Equal-to-the-Apostles Emperor Constantine the Great and his mother Helen.
5-21.bio:
St. Constantine the Great, Equal-to-the-Apostles, was the first Roman Emperor to embrace Christianity. After his vision of the Cross and his victory under its sign, he ended the persecutions with the Edict of Milan, convened the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, and founded Constantinople as a Christian capital. His mother, St. Helen, traveled in old age to the Holy Land, where according to tradition she found the Precious Cross of the Lord and built churches on the holy sites.

Mother and son are commemorated together on May 21, one of the great name days of the Greek world, honored as Equals-to-the-Apostles for turning an empire toward Christ.

5-22.name: Basiliskos
5-22.bio:
The Holy Martyr Basiliskos suffered for Christ in Pontus at the beginning of the fourth century, during the persecutions of the pagan emperors. Tradition remembers him as a kinsman of the Great Martyr Theodore the Recruit and a soldier like him. Refusing to sacrifice to the idols, he endured imprisonment and cruel treatment, and was beheaded at Comana, faithful to the end.

The Church honors in him the courage of the soldier-martyrs who counted loyalty to Christ above life itself. He is commemorated on May 22.

5-23.name: Michael the Confessor
5-23.bio:
St. Michael the Confessor was Bishop of Synnada in Phrygia in the eighth and ninth centuries. A man of holy life, he served the Church in times of trouble and stood firm for the veneration of the holy icons when the iconoclast emperors sought to destroy them. For his confession he was driven from his see and endured exile and hardship until his repose.

The Church names him Confessor because he suffered for the truth without denying it, and honors him among the defenders of the icons. He is commemorated on May 23.

5-24.name: Symeon Stylites
5-24.desc: Venerable Symeon the Stylite of the Younger.
5-24.bio:
St. Symeon the Stylite of the Wonderful Mountain lived in the sixth century near Antioch. Drawn to asceticism from childhood, he took up the rare and severe podvig of the pillar saints, dwelling on a column in fasting, vigil, and unceasing prayer for the greater part of his long life, after the pattern of the first Symeon the Stylite.

From his pillar he taught, counseled, and healed the many who came to him, and was revered as a wonderworker. He is commemorated on May 24.

5-25.name: Third Finding of the Head of John the Baptist
5-25.desc: Third Finding of the Precious Head of John the Baptist.
5-25.bio:
The Church commemorates on May 25 the Third Finding of the honorable head of St. John the Forerunner. According to tradition, the relic had been hidden during the years of iconoclasm; when the veneration of holy things was restored, the head of the Baptist was revealed once more and brought with honor to Constantinople, received by emperor and patriarch amid great rejoicing.

Each finding of the precious head renewed the devotion of the faithful to the Forerunner, the greatest of the prophets and the first preacher of repentance. The feast bears witness to the care of God in preserving the relics of His saints.

5-26.name: Karpos the Apostle
5-26.bio:
The Holy Apostle Karpos was one of the Seventy, a companion and fellow laborer of St. Paul. The Apostle mentions him in his second letter to Timothy, recalling the cloak and books he had left with Karpos at Troas. Tradition holds that he served the Church as a bishop and gave himself wholly to the preaching of the Gospel.

The Church honors him among the apostolic men through whom the faith was planted in the first generation. He is commemorated on May 26.

5-28.name: Helladios
5-28.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Helladios was a bishop of the East in the early centuries of the Church who suffered for Christ in a time of persecution. The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond his faithful service at the altar and his steadfast confession, for which he endured torments and gave his life for the Lord.

The Church keeps his memory among the hieromartyrs, shepherds who laid down their lives for the flock after the example of the Chief Shepherd. He is commemorated on May 28.

5-29.name: Theodosia of Constantinople
5-29.bio:
St. Theodosia was a nun of Constantinople who suffered in the eighth century, at the outbreak of the iconoclast persecution. When the emperor commanded the destruction of the revered icon of Christ above the Chalke Gate of the palace, tradition tells that Theodosia was among the faithful who rose to defend it, and for this she was seized and put to death, sealing her love for Christ with martyrdom.

She was long venerated in Constantinople as a protectress of the city and a helper of the sick. She is commemorated on May 29.

5-30.name: Isaac the Syrian
5-30.desc: Venerable Isaac the Syrian, Bishop of Nineveh.
5-30.bio:
St. Isaac the Syrian lived in the seventh century. A monk from his youth, he was consecrated Bishop of Nineveh, but after only a short time he laid aside the episcopate and withdrew into the desert, giving himself wholly to stillness, prayer, and the study of the Scriptures until blindness and old age overtook him.

His Ascetical Homilies, born of that hidden life, speak of the mercy of God and the humble heart with a depth that has nourished monks and laity alike for centuries. He is commemorated on May 30.

6-1.name: Justin the Philosopher
6-1.bio:
St. Justin the Philosopher and Martyr was born in Palestine and lived in the second century. Seeking truth through the schools of the philosophers, he found it at last in Christ, and thereafter wore the philosopher's cloak in the service of the Gospel. In Rome he wrote his celebrated Apologies, defending the Christians before the emperors and describing the baptism and Eucharist of the early Church.

He was beheaded in Rome with several companions around the year 165, faithful to the truth he had found. The first great Christian apologist, he is commemorated on June 1.

6-2.name: Nikephoros of Constantinople
6-2.desc: Patriarch of Constantinople, defender of icons.
6-2.bio:
St. Nikephoros was Patriarch of Constantinople in the ninth century, in the days when the iconoclast heresy rose a second time. A learned man who had served the empire before taking up the monastic life, he shepherded the Church with wisdom and stood immovably for the veneration of the holy icons. For this he was driven from his throne by the emperor and spent his last years in exile, a confessor for the Orthodox faith.

His relics were later returned to Constantinople with honor, and the Church numbers him among the great defenders of the icons. He is commemorated on June 2.

6-3.name: Lukillian
6-3.bio:
The Holy Martyr Lukillian had been a pagan priest who came to faith in Christ in his old age. Baptized, he confessed the Lord openly and suffered in the third century near Byzantium, enduring torments together with young companions who would not deny Christ, and with them received the crown of martyrdom.

His conversion at the end of a long life given to idols shows that it is never too late to turn to the living God, and that grace can make even an aged newcomer a witness unto blood. He is commemorated on June 3.

6-4.name: Metrophanes of Constantinople
6-4.bio:
St. Metrophanes was the first hierarch of Constantinople, shepherding the Church of Byzantium in the days when St. Constantine the Great made the city his capital. A man of peace and holiness, he guided his flock through the end of the persecutions into the freedom of the Church; by reason of his great age he could not travel to the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, but he upheld its faith.

He reposed in peace soon after, honored by emperor and people alike, and is venerated as the first of the city's long line of archbishops. He is commemorated on June 4.

6-5.name: Dorotheus of Tyre
6-5.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Dorotheus was Bishop of Tyre in Phoenicia. He suffered exile in the great persecution under Diocletian, returned to his flock in the peace of the Church, and shepherded them for many years as a learned and holy elder. In extreme old age, tradition tells, he was seized in the days of Julian the Apostate and died a martyr from the torments inflicted on him.

The Church honors him as a shepherd who served through persecution, peace, and persecution again, faithful across a whole century of the Church's life. He is commemorated on June 5.

6-6.name: Hilarion the New
6-6.bio:
St. Hilarion the New was abbot of the Dalmaton monastery in Constantinople in the ninth century. A monk of strict life and deep humility, he guided his brotherhood in the ways of prayer and obedience, and when the iconoclast emperors renewed their war on the holy icons he refused to submit, enduring imprisonment and exile for the sake of the Orthodox faith.

He is honored as a confessor, one of the monastic fathers whose steadfastness preserved the veneration of the icons until its final restoration. He is commemorated on June 6.

6-7.name: Theodotus of Ancyra
6-7.bio:
The Holy Martyr Theodotus of Ancyra suffered under the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. An innkeeper by trade, he used his house and his means to shelter persecuted Christians, to care for prisoners, and to give burial to the bodies of the martyrs when it was forbidden. For this holy boldness he was himself seized, tortured, and beheaded.

The Church remembers in him a layman whose ordinary trade became a ministry of mercy, and whose mercy became martyrdom. He is commemorated on June 7.

6-8.name: Theodore Stratelates
6-8.desc: Translation of relics of Theodore Stratelates.
6-8.bio:
The Holy Great Martyr Theodore Stratelates, the Commander, was a military governor in Asia Minor who suffered for Christ under the emperor Licinius at the beginning of the fourth century. Confessing the Lord openly and overturning the worship of idols, he endured cruel tortures and was beheaded, encouraging the faithful to stand firm.

On June 8 the Church commemorates the translation of his relics to his family home at Euchaita, according to his own dying wish. With St. Theodore the Recruit he is one of the two beloved warrior saints named Theodore, invoked by soldiers and honored throughout the Orthodox world.

6-11.name: Kyrilos and Methodios
6-11.desc: Holy Equal-to-the-Apostles Cyril and Methodios, enlighteners of the Slavs.
6-11.bio:
Sts. Cyril and Methodios, Equals-to-the-Apostles, were brothers from Thessaloniki in the ninth century. Learned and devout, they were sent from Constantinople as missionaries to the Slavic peoples; for their sake they devised an alphabet for the Slavonic tongue and translated the Scriptures and the divine services, so that the people could worship God in their own language.
