Their labors bore fruit in the conversion of whole nations, and they are honored as the enlighteners of the Slavs and patrons of Slavic letters. They are commemorated on June 11.

6-12.name: Onuphrios the Great
6-12.bio:
St. Onuphrios the Great was one of the greatest hermits of the Egyptian desert, living in the fourth century. Leaving his monastery for the inner wilderness, he dwelt alone for some sixty years in utter poverty, unseen by men, clothed only in his own hair and a girdle of leaves, sustained by God in prayer.

Near the end of his life he was discovered by the monk Paphnutios, who heard his story, witnessed his blessed repose, and made his life known to the Church. He is loved as an image of total surrender to God, and is commemorated on June 12.

6-13.name: Aquilina
6-13.bio:
The Holy Martyr Aquilina was a young girl of Byblos in Phoenicia who suffered under the persecution of Diocletian at the end of the third century. Raised in the faith from infancy, she spoke of Christ to her companions with such boldness that she was denounced to the authorities, and though only a child she endured torments and death rather than deny the Lord.

The Church honors in her the courage of the young, whose purity of faith puts the mighty to shame. She is commemorated on June 13.

6-14.name: Eliseos the Prophet
6-14.bio:
The Holy Prophet Elisha lived in the ninth century before Christ. Called from the plough by the Prophet Elijah, he left all to follow him, and when Elijah was taken up in the fiery chariot Elisha received his mantle and a double portion of his spirit. He prophesied in Israel for many years, working great wonders: healing the waters, multiplying the widow's oil, cleansing Naaman the leper, and raising the dead.

The Church honors him among the greatest of the prophets, a man of God through whom the power of the Lord was shown to a wayward people. He is commemorated on June 14.

6-15.name: Amos the Prophet
6-15.bio:
The Holy Prophet Amos was a shepherd and dresser of sycamore trees from Tekoa, called by God in the eighth century before Christ to prophesy to the northern kingdom of Israel. A plain man with no schooling of the prophets, he spoke fearlessly against the injustice of the rich and the emptiness of worship without righteousness, declaring the word of the Lord: let justice roll down like waters.

His book stands among the twelve minor prophets, and the Church honors him as a voice of God's righteousness. He is commemorated on June 15.

6-16.name: Tychon of Amathus
6-16.bio:
St. Tychon was Bishop of Amathus in Cyprus in the fifth century. The son of a baker, he was known from youth for his generosity to the poor, and as bishop he labored with apostolic zeal to turn the remaining pagans of the island from their idols to Christ, shepherding his flock with gentleness and prayer.

He was glorified as a wonderworker both in life and after his repose, and has been venerated in Cyprus from ancient times as one of the island's own saints. He is commemorated on June 16.

6-17.name: Isauros and companions
6-17.bio:
The Holy Martyr Isauros, a deacon, suffered for Christ in the early centuries of the Church together with a company of fellow believers. Refusing to deny the Lord, they strengthened one another in prison and went together to their deaths, sealing their confession with their blood.

The synaxaria preserve little more of their story, but the Church keeps their memory among the companies of martyrs who stood side by side in the hour of trial. They are commemorated on June 17.

6-18.name: Leontios
6-18.bio:
The Holy Martyr Leontios was a soldier of Greek descent who suffered for Christ at Tripoli in Phoenicia in the early centuries of the Church. A man of courage and charity, he confessed the Lord before his accusers, and tradition tells that his steadfastness under torment brought even those sent against him to faith in Christ, so that they shared his martyrdom.

He was venerated at Tripoli from ancient times, and churches in his honor spread through the East. He is commemorated on June 18.

6-21.name: Iouliane and Barnabas
6-21.bio:
The Holy Martyrs commemorated on this day suffered for Christ in the early centuries of the Church. Of their lives the synaxaria preserve little beyond their faithful confession: that in a time of persecution they refused to deny the Lord and gave their lives rather than betray Him.

The Church keeps their memory among the great cloud of witnesses whose names are written in heaven, honoring in them the victory of faith over death. They are commemorated on June 21.

6-22.name: Eusebios of Samosata
6-22.bio:
St. Eusebios, Bishop of Samosata, was one of the great champions of the Nicene faith in the fourth century, a friend and fellow struggler of St. Basil the Great. In the years when Arianism held the empire, he traveled through the East, tradition says even in disguise, strengthening the faithful and ordaining Orthodox clergy, and for this he was driven into exile under the emperor Valens.

Returning after the persecution eased, he met a martyr's end around the year 380, struck down by a tile hurled by a woman of the heretics as he entered a city to install an Orthodox bishop. He is commemorated on June 22.

6-23.name: Agrippina
6-23.bio:
The Holy Martyr Agrippina was a Christian maiden of Rome who suffered for Christ in the third century. Raised in piety, she adorned herself not with gold but with chastity and prayer, and when persecution came she confessed the Lord openly and died under torture rather than deny Him.

Her holy relics were carried by devout women to Sicily, where her veneration flourished from ancient times and many miracles were ascribed to her intercession. She is commemorated on June 23.

6-24.name: Nativity of John the Baptist
6-24.desc: Nativity of the Holy Forerunner and Baptist John.
6-24.bio:
The Nativity of St. John the Forerunner is celebrated on June 24, six months before the Nativity of Christ. The Gospel of Luke recounts how the Archangel Gabriel announced to the aged priest Zacharias that his barren wife Elizabeth would bear a son; struck mute for his doubt, Zacharias regained his speech at the naming of the child and prophesied that the boy would be called the prophet of the Most High.

John was born to prepare the way of the Lord, and his birth was itself the beginning of the joy of the Gospel. The Church keeps the feast as one of the great celebrations of the Forerunner.

6-25.name: Febronia
6-25.bio:
St. Febronia was a young nun of Mesopotamia who suffered for Christ at the beginning of the fourth century, in the persecution of Diocletian. Raised in a monastery from childhood, she was famed for her beauty, her wisdom, and her love of the Scriptures. When the persecutors seized her, she refused the offer of marriage and freedom in exchange for denying Christ, and endured a cruel martyrdom with unbroken faith.

Her contest, recorded by the nuns who knew her, made her one of the most venerated virgin-martyrs of the East. She is commemorated on June 25.

6-26.name: David of Thessaloniki
6-26.bio:
St. David of Thessaloniki was an ascetic of the sixth century who lived in that city as a stranger to the world. Tradition tells that he made his dwelling in the branches of an almond tree, enduring heat and cold for years in prayer, until God revealed that his petition was heard; thereafter he lived in a cell, where the faithful sought his prayers and counsel, and he was granted the grace of wonderworking.

He is one of the beloved patron saints of Thessaloniki, where his relics are venerated to this day. He is commemorated on June 26.

6-27.name: Sampson the Hospitable
6-27.desc: Venerable Samson the Hospitable of Constantinople.
6-27.bio:
St. Sampson the Hospitable was a physician of noble birth who settled in Constantinople in the days of the emperor Justinian. Ordained a priest, he gave his skill and his wealth to the sick and the poor, receiving them into his own house; tradition tells that he healed the emperor himself, and with imperial help there arose the great hospice that bore his name for centuries, one of the famed houses of Christian mercy in the city.

He is honored among the unmercenary physicians, a father of Christian medicine and philanthropy. He is commemorated on June 27.

6-29.name: Peter and Paul the Apostles
6-29.desc: Feast of the Chief Apostles Peter and Paul.
6-29.bio:
The feast of Sts. Peter and Paul honors together the two chief Apostles. St. Peter, the fisherman of Galilee who confessed Christ as the Son of the living God, was foremost among the Twelve and, after his denial and restoration, strengthened the brethren and preached to the end. St. Paul, once a persecutor of the Church, was converted by the risen Christ on the road to Damascus and became the Apostle to the Nations.

According to tradition both were martyred in Rome under Nero, Peter by crucifixion and Paul by the sword. Their feast on June 29 crowns the Apostles Fast and is a cherished name day for Petros and Pavlos.

6-30.name: Synaxis of the Holy Apostles
6-30.desc: Synaxis of the Glorious and All-Praised Twelve Apostles.
6-30.bio:
On the day after the feast of Sts. Peter and Paul, the Church celebrates in one synaxis the Twelve Apostles of Christ. Chosen by the Lord to be with Him and to be sent out to preach, they received the Holy Spirit at Pentecost and carried the Gospel to the ends of the known world, nearly all of them sealing their witness with martyrdom.

The Church is called apostolic because it rests upon their preaching and continues their mission. The synaxis on June 30 gathers into one commemoration the men through whom the good news of the Resurrection was first proclaimed in every land.

7-1.name: Kosmas and Damian of Rome
7-1.desc: Holy Unmercenary Physicians Cosmas and Damian of Rome.
7-1.bio:
Sts. Kosmas and Damian of Rome were brothers and physicians of the third century who healed the sick freely in the name of Christ, accepting no payment, for which they are counted among the Holy Unmercenaries. Their charity and their faith drew many to the Church, and according to tradition they ended their lives as martyrs.

They are distinguished in the calendar from the other holy Unmercenaries of the same names honored in November and October. Physicians and the sick alike seek their intercession. They are commemorated on July 1.

7-2.name: Juvenaly of Jerusalem
7-2.bio:
St. Juvenaly was Patriarch of Jerusalem in the fifth century, shepherding the Holy City for several decades during the great christological controversies. He took part in the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus and the Fourth at Chalcedon, standing with the Orthodox faith in Christ, and during his episcopate the see of Jerusalem was honored as a patriarchate.

Tradition also associates him with the events surrounding the veneration of the Dormition of the Theotokos. He reposed in peace after a long ministry, and is commemorated on July 2.

7-3.name: Hyakinthos
7-3.bio:
St. Hyakinthos was a young Christian of Caesarea in Cappadocia who served at the imperial court in the time of the Emperor Trajan. When his faith became known, he refused to eat food offered to idols, and for his confession of Christ he was imprisoned and died in his bonds, still in his youth, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

His steadfastness at so young an age has made him an example of purity of conscience, keeping the faith even in small things. He is commemorated on July 3.

7-4.name: Andrew the Apostle of Crete
7-4.bio:
St. Andrew of Crete was born in Damascus in the seventh century. First a monk in Jerusalem, he later served in Constantinople and was consecrated Archbishop of Gortyna in Crete, where he shepherded his flock with wisdom and care for the poor.

He is honored above all as a hymnographer, the author of the Great Canon of repentance, which the Church sings during Great Lent as one of her most profound calls to compunction. He reposed in the first half of the eighth century and is commemorated on July 4.

7-5.name: Athanasios of Athos
7-5.desc: Founder of the Great Lavra of Mount Athos.
7-5.bio:
St. Athanasios the Athonite was born in Trebizond in the tenth century. Drawn from a promising career in Constantinople to the monastic life, he came to Mount Athos and there founded the Great Lavra, the first of the great communal monasteries of the Holy Mountain, with the support of the Emperor Nikephoros Phokas.

Under his guidance Athos grew into the chief center of Orthodox monasticism, as it remains to this day. According to tradition he ended his earthly life during the collapse of a church structure under construction at the Lavra. He is commemorated on July 5.

7-6.name: Sisoes the Great
7-6.bio:
St. Sisoes the Great was one of the renowned desert fathers of Egypt, living in the fourth and fifth centuries. After years in Sketis he withdrew to the mountain where St. Anthony the Great had lived, and there spent long decades in solitude, prayer, and profound humility, receiving those who came for a word of salvation.

His sayings, preserved among the fathers, breathe repentance and gentleness; at the end of his life he confessed that he did not know if he had even begun to repent. He is commemorated on July 6.

7-7.name: Thomas of Maloea
7-7.bio:
St. Thomas of Maloea was, according to tradition, a man of prominence and strength in the world who left all things to become a monk, taking up the life of prayer and ascetic struggle on Mount Maloea. There he lived in stillness, and God glorified his hidden labors with the grace of wonderworking.

The synaxaria preserve little else of his life beyond his renunciation of the world and his holiness in the desert. He is commemorated on July 7.

7-8.name: Procopios
7-8.bio:
St. Procopios the Great Martyr suffered for Christ at Caesarea in Palestine during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. According to tradition he was first a persecutor of Christians, but was converted by a divine revelation, confessed Christ openly, and endured imprisonment and torture before being beheaded.

He is numbered among the great military martyrs of the Church, and many churches in the Greek world bear his name. His feast is kept on July 8.

7-9.name: Pancratius of Tauromenion
7-9.bio:
St. Pancratius was, according to tradition, a disciple of the apostles who was sent to Sicily and became the first bishop of Tauromenium, present-day Taormina. There he preached the Gospel, overturned the worship of idols, and gathered a flock for Christ in the earliest days of the Church.

He completed his ministry as a martyr, put to death by enemies of the faith. He is honored as one of the apostolic founders of the Church in Sicily, and is commemorated on July 9.

7-10.name: Anthony of the Kiev Caves
7-10.desc: Venerable Anthony of the Kiev Far Caves, founder of monasticism in Rus′ (†1073).
7-10.bio:
St. Anthony of the Kiev Caves is honored as the father of monasticism in the lands of Rus. Born at Lyubech, he received the monastic tonsure on Mount Athos, and returning north he settled in a cave above the Dnieper River near Kiev, where his holiness drew disciples and the great Monastery of the Caves took root.

With his disciple St. Theodosius he set the pattern of monastic life that shaped the piety of Rus for centuries. He reposed in 1073 and is commemorated on July 10.

7-10.name: Forty-Five Holy Martyrs of Nicopolis
7-10.desc: The Forty-Five Holy Martyrs of Nicopolis in Armenia, martyred under Licinius (c. 319).
7-10.bio:
The Forty-Five Holy Martyrs of Nicopolis in Armenia confessed Christ during the persecution of the Emperor Licinius, around the year 319. Presenting themselves openly as Christians, they were imprisoned and endured harsh sufferings, encouraging one another in prayer and psalmody, and were finally put to death by fire.

Their shared confession, offered freely and together, has made them an image of the strength of the faithful united in Christ. They are commemorated on July 10.

7-10.name: Amalia
7-10.desc: Name day for Amalia and Amelie in the Greek Orthodox tradition, commemorated with the Martyrs of Nicopolis.
7-10.bio:
In the Greek Orthodox tradition, those who bear the name Amalia keep their name day on July 10, together with the commemoration of the Forty-Five Holy Martyrs of Nicopolis. The name, of old Germanic origin, carries the sense of industriousness and care, and came into Greek usage in more recent centuries.

On this day those named Amalia and Amelie are remembered in the prayers of the Church along with the holy martyrs, whose steadfast confession of Christ sanctifies the day. The commemoration is kept on July 10.

7-11.name: Euphemia the All-Praised
7-11.bio:
St. Euphemia the All-Praised was a virgin martyr of Chalcedon who suffered for Christ during the persecutions at the turn of the fourth century, enduring torture and death rather than sacrifice to idols. Her principal feast is kept on September 16.

On July 11 the Church commemorates the miracle wrought through her relics at the Fourth Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon in 451, when, according to tradition, the definition of the Orthodox faith placed in her tomb was received and confirmed, sealing the true confession of Christ. For this she is called the confirmer of Orthodoxy, and is honored on July 11.

7-12.name: Proclos of Constantinople
7-12.bio:
St. Proclos was a disciple of St. John Chrysostom and served as Patriarch of Constantinople in the fifth century. A gentle and eloquent shepherd, he taught the faith with clarity, honored the Theotokos in his celebrated homilies, and brought the relics of his teacher Chrysostom back to Constantinople with great solemnity, healing an old wound in the Church.

Tradition also connects his patriarchate with the establishment of the Trisagion hymn in the services of the Church. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on July 12.

7-30.name: Silas the Apostle
7-30.desc: Holy Apostle Silas, companion of Paul.
7-30.bio:
St. Silas, numbered among the Seventy Apostles, was a leading man of the Church in Jerusalem who was chosen to accompany St. Paul on his missionary journeys. He shared the Apostle's labors and sufferings, and at Philippi was imprisoned with him, praying and singing hymns at midnight when the earthquake opened the prison doors.

According to tradition he later served as bishop of Corinth, completing his apostolic course in faithfulness. He is commemorated with his fellow apostles on July 30.

7-14.name: Aquila the Apostle
7-14.bio:
St. Aquila, numbered among the Seventy Apostles, was a Jewish tentmaker who with his wife Priscilla received St. Paul into their home at Corinth and shared both his trade and his labors for the Gospel. The couple are mentioned with affection in the Scriptures, and their house served as a gathering place for the Church.

According to tradition Aquila preached the Gospel and was made a bishop, ending his life in martyrdom. He is commemorated on July 14.

7-15.name: Vladimir of Kiev
7-15.desc: Equal-to-the-Apostles Vladimir, Great Prince of Kiev.
7-15.bio:
St. Vladimir, Equal-to-the-Apostles, was Great Prince of Kiev in the tenth century. Raised in paganism, he sought out the true faith, and after his envoys beheld the divine services in Constantinople he received holy baptism and in 988 led his people to the waters of the Dnieper, the baptism of Rus.

From a harsh ruler he became a father to his people, building churches, feeding the poor, and softening the laws. Through him the Orthodox faith took root in the lands of Rus. He reposed in 1015 and is commemorated on July 15.

7-16.name: Athenogenes
7-16.bio:
St. Athenogenes was a bishop in the region of Sebaste who suffered martyrdom with a company of his disciples during the persecutions at the turn of the fourth century. Refusing to deny Christ, he strengthened his spiritual children as they went before him to death, and then received the crown of martyrdom himself.

An ancient tradition tells that as he went to his death he sang with joy, and his name is linked in the memory of the Church with the beloved evening hymn of thanksgiving at the lighting of the lamps. He is commemorated on July 16.

7-17.name: Marina the Great Martyr
7-17.bio:
St. Marina the Great Martyr was born in Antioch of Pisidia in the third century. Losing her mother as a child and raised in the countryside, she embraced Christ in her youth; when her faith became known she was seized during the persecutions, and though only about fifteen years of age she withstood interrogation, torture, and, according to tradition, the assaults of the evil one, whom she overcame by prayer, before being beheaded.

She is greatly beloved in Greece, where many churches and villages bear her name, and she is invoked as a protector of children and a help against the powers of darkness. Her feast is July 17.

7-18.name: Emilian of Dorostolum
7-18.bio:
St. Emilian was a Christian of Dorostolon on the Danube who suffered martyrdom in the fourth century, in the reign of Julian the Apostate. Moved by zeal for the true God, he entered a pagan temple and overturned the idols; when another man was blamed for the deed, he came forward and confessed it freely rather than let the innocent suffer.

For his confession of Christ he was put to death by fire, and the Church honors his honesty and courage together. He is commemorated on July 18.

7-19.name: Makrina the Elder
7-19.desc: Venerable Macrina, grandmother of Basil the Great.
7-19.bio:
St. Makrina belonged to the extraordinary Cappadocian family of saints that gave the Church St. Basil the Great and St. Gregory of Nyssa. A woman of deep piety and steadfast faith, she devoted herself to prayer and the ascetic life, and through her teaching and example the Orthodox faith was handed down within a household that produced some of the greatest fathers of the Church.

She is honored as a model of holiness lived out in family life, showing how the faith is passed from generation to generation. She is commemorated on July 19.

7-20.name: Elijah the Prophet
7-20.desc: Holy Prophet Elijah the Tishbite, taken up to heaven in a fiery chariot.
7-20.bio:
The Holy Prophet Elijah the Tishbite lived in the ninth century before Christ, in the days of King Ahab of Israel. Zealous for the Lord against the worship of Baal, he shut the heavens by his prayer, was fed by ravens at the brook Cherith, raised the son of the widow of Zarephath, and called down fire from heaven on Mount Carmel. He was taken up alive toward heaven in a chariot of fire, leaving his mantle to his disciple Elisha.

Elijah appeared with Moses beside Christ at the Transfiguration. In Greece his chapels crown countless mountaintops, and his feast on July 20 is kept with great devotion.

7-21.name: Symeon the Fool for Christ
7-21.desc: Venerable Symeon the Holy Fool for Christ.
7-21.bio:
St. Symeon the Fool for Christ was a sixth-century ascetic of Syria. After long years of prayer and struggle in the desert by the Dead Sea with his companion St. John, he was called to a stranger path: entering the city of Emesa, he feigned madness, enduring mockery and blows while secretly feeding the poor, converting sinners, and working hidden wonders.

His folly concealed great holiness, revealed only after his repose. He is honored as one of the first and greatest of the fools for Christ, and is commemorated on July 21.

7-22.name: Mary Magdalene
7-22.bio:
St. Mary Magdalene, the Myrrh-Bearer and Equal-to-the-Apostles, was healed by the Lord of seven demons and thereafter followed Him from Galilee, ministering to Him from her own means. She stood by the Cross when most had fled, and coming early to the tomb she was among the first to behold the risen Christ, who sent her to announce the Resurrection to the Apostles.

For this she is honored as an apostle to the apostles. According to tradition she later preached the Gospel and reposed in Ephesus, and her relics were brought in time to Constantinople. The Church commemorates her on July 22 and with the Myrrh-Bearers after Pascha.

7-22.name: Phokas of Sinope
7-22.bio:
St. Phokas was bishop of Sinope on the Black Sea, a shepherd of the early Church renowned for his holiness, who completed his ministry as a hieromartyr, suffering death for his confession of Christ during the Roman persecutions.

He has long been honored as a protector of seafarers, and sailors of the Black Sea and beyond kept his memory with special devotion. Alongside his principal feast in September, the Church also commemorates him on July 22, the day associated with the translation of his holy relics.

7-22.name: Markella of Chios
7-22.bio:
St. Markella was a young virgin of the island of Chios, honored by tradition as a martyr of purity. Raised in the faith by a devout mother whom she lost early, she lived in prayer and modesty. When her own father, given over to sinful passion, pursued her, she fled; refusing to yield, she was put to death by his hand and received the crown of martyrdom.

At the place of her martyrdom on Chios a shrine and holy spring bear her memory, and many pilgrims seek her intercession there. She is the patroness of Chios, and her feast is kept on July 22.

7-23.name: Ezekiel the Prophet
7-23.bio:
The Holy Prophet Ezekiel was a priest of Israel carried into the Babylonian captivity in the sixth century before Christ. By the river Chebar he beheld the awesome vision of the glory of the Lord upon the chariot of the cherubim, and he prophesied to the exiles both judgment and consolation, including the vision of the dry bones brought to life, a foreshadowing of the resurrection.

The Church reads his prophecy of the shut gate as a figure of the Ever-Virgin Theotokos. He is commemorated on July 23.

7-24.name: Christina the Great Martyr
7-24.bio:
St. Christina the Great Martyr suffered for Christ at Tyre in the third century. Born to a prominent pagan family and kept apart by her father, she came to knowledge of the one true God, and destroyed the idols of gold and silver set before her, giving the fragments to the poor. For this she endured imprisonment and cruel tortures at the hands of successive judges, remaining unshaken until she received the crown of martyrdom.

Her name proclaims her belonging to Christ, and her courage in her youth has been honored throughout the centuries. Her feast is July 24.

7-25.name: Dormition of Anne
7-25.desc: Dormition of Saint Anne, mother of the Theotokos.
7-25.bio:
On July 25 the Church commemorates the Dormition of St. Anna, the mother of the Most Holy Theotokos. With her husband, the righteous Joachim, she bore childlessness with patience and prayer until God granted them in old age the daughter who would become the Mother of God. According to tradition she reposed in peace in Jerusalem.

St. Anna is honored as the grandmother of Christ according to the flesh, and is invoked by mothers, by married couples, and by those praying to be granted children. The feast is the principal name day of those named Anna.

7-26.name: Paraskevi the Great Martyr
7-26.bio:
St. Paraskevi was born near Rome in the second century to devout Christian parents, who named her for the day of the Passion of the Lord, Friday, in Greek Paraskevi. After their death she gave her goods to the poor and went about preaching Christ, for which she was arrested; she endured torture with steadfastness and was finally beheaded, her witness, according to tradition, bringing even her persecutors to wonder.

She is one of the most beloved women saints of Greece, and because tradition tells of healing granted through her to the eyes of a persecutor, she is invoked especially for diseases of sight. Her feast is July 26.

7-27.name: Panteleimon the Unmercenary
7-27.desc: Great Martyr and Unmercenary Panteleimon of Nicomedia.
7-27.bio:
St. Panteleimon the Great Martyr and Healer was born in Nicomedia in the late third century. Trained as a physician, he was brought to Christ by the priest St. Hermolaos, and thereafter healed the sick freely in the name of the Lord, taking no payment, for which he is counted among the Holy Unmercenaries. Denounced during the persecution of Maximian, he endured many tortures and was beheaded around the year 305.

His name means all-merciful. He is invoked above all for the sick, and physicians and nurses honor him as their patron. His feast on July 27 is kept with devotion throughout the Orthodox world.

7-28.name: Prokoros the Apostle
7-28.bio:
St. Prokoros was one of the Seven Deacons chosen by the Apostles in Jerusalem to serve the needs of the growing Church, as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. According to tradition he became a devoted disciple and companion of St. John the Theologian, accompanying him in his labors and, as tradition holds, serving as his scribe.

He is said to have later served as bishop of Nicomedia and to have completed his course as a martyr. He is commemorated on July 28.

7-29.name: Kallinikos
7-29.bio:
St. Kallinikos was a Christian of Asia Minor who traveled from place to place preaching Christ and turning many from the worship of idols. Seized during the persecutions, he was brought to Gangra in Paphlagonia, where after cruel torments he was condemned to death by fire, and gave up his soul to God with thanksgiving.

His name means one of beautiful victory, and the Church honors in him the triumph of faith over suffering. He is commemorated on July 29.

8-1.name: Beginning of the Dormition Fast
8-1.desc: Beginning of the Dormition Fast — Procession of the Cross.
8-1.bio:
On the first of August the Church enters the Dormition Fast, two weeks of fasting and prayer in preparation for the great feast of the Dormition of the Theotokos on August 15. During these days the faithful gather in the evenings for the Paraklesis, the supplicatory canon to the Mother of God, seeking her intercession.

On this day the Church also keeps the Procession of the Precious Cross, an observance from Constantinople in which the Cross was carried forth for the blessing and protection of the people. The fast begins on August 1.

8-1.name: Elesa of Kythira
8-1.desc: Holy Virgin-Martyr Elesa, patron saint of Kythira and protector of childbirth and expectant mothers.
8-1.bio:
St. Elesa was a virgin martyr honored by tradition as the patroness of the island of Kythira. Her very birth was an answer to prayer: her mother, a pious Christian who had long struggled to bear a child, prayed fervently and received the divine assurance that God had shown her mercy — in Greek, ho Theos elesese — and so the daughter granted to her was named Elesa. Raised by her mother in the faith despite her pagan father, she embraced Christ and consecrated her life to Him. When her father raged against her faith she fled across the water to Kythira; pursuing her there, he put her to death, and she received the crown of martyrdom in her youth.

Because her own birth was God's answer to a childless mother's prayer, St. Elesa is venerated as a protector of childbirth and of expectant mothers, who seek her intercession for the gift of children and a safe delivery. On the mountain of Kythira where tradition places her martyrdom stands the monastery that bears her name, a place of pilgrimage for the islanders. Her feast is celebrated on August 1.

8-3.name: Phokas the Gardener
8-3.bio:
St. Phokas the Gardener lived near Sinope on the Black Sea, cultivating a small garden by the city gate and giving freely of its produce to the poor and to travelers, whom he received with open hospitality. In a time of persecution, soldiers were sent to find and kill the Christian Phokas; unknowing, they lodged with him, and he, having prepared his own grave in the night, revealed himself in the morning and received death for Christ.

He has long been honored as a patron of gardeners and of seafarers. He is commemorated on August 3.

8-4.name: Seven Youths of Ephesus
8-4.bio:
The Seven Holy Youths of Ephesus were young Christians of noble standing who, during the persecution of the Emperor Decius in the third century, took refuge in a cave outside the city rather than sacrifice to idols. There, by the providence of God, they fell into a wondrous sleep, and the cave was sealed.

Generations later, in the days of the Emperor Theodosius the Younger, they were found alive, a living witness against those who doubted the resurrection of the dead. Having borne this testimony, they reposed in peace. They are commemorated on August 4.

8-5.name: Eusignios
8-5.bio:
St. Eusignios was a soldier of Antioch who served long years in the Roman armies, and according to tradition had served under Constantine the Great and beheld the appearing of the sign of the Cross. In extreme old age, in the reign of Julian the Apostate, he was denounced as a Christian; brought before the emperor, he boldly rebuked his apostasy and confessed Christ, for which he was beheaded.

His martyrdom in old age crowned a lifetime of faithfulness. He is commemorated on August 5.

8-6.name: Transfiguration of the Lord
8-6.desc: The Holy Transfiguration of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
8-6.bio:
The Great Feast of the Transfiguration commemorates the day Christ led Peter, James, and John up Mount Tabor and was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, His garments became white as light, Moses and Elijah appeared speaking with Him, and the voice of the Father declared Him the beloved Son.

The feast, kept on August 6 in the midst of the Dormition Fast, reveals the uncreated light of the divinity of Christ and the glory to which the human person is called. In Greek tradition the first grapes of the harvest are brought to church on this day to be blessed.

8-7.name: Dometios the Persian
8-7.bio:
St. Dometios was a Persian of the fourth century who came to faith in Christ and left his homeland for the regions of Syria and Mesopotamia, where he received the monastic tonsure and later lived in ascetic solitude, drawing many who sought healing and counsel through his prayers.

In the reign of Julian the Apostate he was put to death for Christ, stoned, according to tradition, together with two disciples. He is commemorated on August 7.

8-8.name: Emilian the Confessor
8-8.bio:
St. Emilian was bishop of Cyzicus in the ninth century, during the renewed persecution of the holy icons. Summoned to reject the veneration of the icons of Christ and the saints, he refused, defending the Orthodox faith with firmness before the iconoclast emperor.

For his confession he was driven from his see and endured exile and hardship until his blessed repose, receiving the title of Confessor from the Church he would not betray. He is commemorated on August 8.

8-9.name: Matthias the Apostle
8-9.desc: Holy Apostle Matthias chosen to replace Judas.
8-9.bio:
St. Matthias was a disciple of the Lord from the beginning, one of those who accompanied Him from the baptism of John until the Ascension. After the fall of Judas, the Apostles prayed and cast lots, and Matthias was chosen to take his place among the Twelve, as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles.

According to tradition he preached the Gospel with boldness and completed his apostolic course as a martyr. He is commemorated on August 9.

8-10.name: Lawrence the Archdeacon
8-10.bio:
St. Lawrence was archdeacon of the Church of Rome in the third century, entrusted with her treasury and her care for the poor. In the persecution of Valerian, when the prefect demanded the treasures of the Church, Lawrence gathered the poor and the sick and presented them, saying that these were her treasures.

For this he was put to a cruel death by fire in the year 258, enduring, according to tradition, with unbroken and even joyful courage. His martyrdom is honored in both East and West, and he is commemorated on August 10.

8-11.name: Euphrosyne
8-11.bio:
St. Euphrosyne of Alexandria was the only daughter of a wealthy and devout father in the fifth century. Desiring the monastic life and fleeing an arranged marriage, she secretly left her home and, concealing her identity in a men's monastery, spent many years in prayer, fasting, and hidden struggle.

Near the end of her life she was revealed to her own father, who had long mourned her, and who himself then took up the monastic life in her cell. She is commemorated on August 11.

8-22.name: Phokas of Sinope (Bishop)
8-22.desc: Holy Hieromartyr Phocas, Bishop of Sinope.
8-22.bio:
St. Phokas served as bishop of Sinope on the Black Sea in the early centuries of the Church, shepherding his flock with holiness during the age of persecutions. Remaining faithful to Christ, he was put to death for his confession and is honored as a hieromartyr.

From ancient times he has been venerated as a protector of those who sail the seas, and churches along the coasts were dedicated to his name. In addition to his principal feast in September, his memory is also kept on August 22.

8-22.name: Agathonikis
8-22.bio:
St. Agathonike was a martyr of the early Church who confessed Christ during the Roman persecutions and laid down her life rather than deny her Lord. The synaxaria preserve little of her beyond her faithful confession and her endurance to the end.

Her memory is kept together with the company of martyrs honored on this day, and those who bear the name Agathoniki celebrate their name day in her honor. She is commemorated on August 22.

8-13.name: Maximos the Confessor
8-13.bio:
St. Maximos the Confessor was a monk and theologian of the seventh century. Leaving high office in Constantinople for the monastic life, he became the great defender of the true faith against monothelitism, teaching that Christ, being true God and true man, possesses both a divine and a human will. For refusing to keep silence he was tried, mutilated, and exiled, dying in banishment in 662.

His profound writings on theology and the spiritual life remain treasures of the Church. His principal feast is January 21; on August 13 the Church commemorates the translation of his relics.

8-15.name: Dormition of the Theotokos
8-15.desc: The Dormition (Falling Asleep) of our Most Holy Lady the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary.
8-15.bio:
The Great Feast of the Dormition commemorates the falling asleep of the Most Holy Theotokos. According to tradition, the Apostles were gathered from the ends of the earth to her bedside in Jerusalem, where she gave her soul into the hands of her Son; her body was laid in a tomb in Gethsemane and was found to have been taken up, for the Mother of Life was translated to life.

Kept on August 15 at the close of the two-week Dormition Fast, this is the greatest of the feasts of the Theotokos — the Pascha of summer, as it is called in Greek tradition — and the name day of Maria, Panagiota, and Despina.

8-16.name: Translation of Mandylion
8-16.desc: Translation of the Not-Made-by-Hands Icon (Mandylion) to Constantinople.
8-16.bio:
This feast commemorates the translation of the Holy Mandylion, the Icon of Christ Not-Made-by-Hands, from Edessa to Constantinople in the tenth century. According to tradition, King Abgar of Edessa, suffering from illness, sent to the Lord asking for healing, and received a cloth upon which the face of Christ had been imprinted without human hands; through it he was healed and believed.

The Mandylion was treasured in Edessa for centuries and brought with great honor to Constantinople on August 16. The feast celebrates Christ as the true image of God made visible in the flesh, and stands at the foundation of the Orthodox veneration of icons.

8-17.name: Myron of Crete
8-17.bio:
St. Myron was bishop of Crete, remembered as a wonderworker and a man of great compassion. A farmer before his episcopacy, he was famed for his generosity; tradition tells that finding thieves in his threshing floor, he helped them load their sacks and let them depart, winning them by kindness.

As bishop he shepherded the Church of Crete with the same mercy, and God glorified him with the grace of miracles. He reposed in old age and is commemorated on August 17.

8-18.name: Floros and Lavros
8-18.bio:
Sts. Floros and Lavros were brothers, stonemasons by trade, who labored in Illyricum in the early centuries of the Church. Hired to build a pagan temple, they gave their wages to the poor, and when the work was done they gathered the poor together, overturned the idols, and consecrated the building to Christ. For this they were put to death, according to tradition cast into a well.

Their memory has been kept with love among the Orthodox peoples, and in Slavic tradition they are honored as protectors of horses. They are commemorated on August 18.

8-19.name: Andrew the General
8-19.bio:
St. Andrew Stratelates was a commander in the Roman army in the East at the end of the third century. Calling on the name of Christ, he led his soldiers to victory, and confessed openly the faith that had given it; many of his men believed with him and were baptized.

Denounced during the persecution of Maximian, he and a great company of his fellow soldiers withdrew to the mountains of Cilicia, where they were overtaken and slain, receiving together the crown of martyrdom. He is commemorated on August 19.

8-20.name: Samuel the Prophet
8-20.bio:
The Holy Prophet Samuel was the last of the judges of Israel, born in answer to the prayers of his mother Hannah, who dedicated him to God from childhood. Serving in the sanctuary at Shiloh, he heard the call of the Lord as a boy, and grew to be a faithful prophet, judging Israel in righteousness.

At God's command he anointed Saul as the first king of Israel, and afterward David, the ancestor of Christ according to the flesh. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on August 20.

8-21.name: Thaddaeus the Apostle
8-21.bio:
St. Thaddaeus, numbered among the Seventy Apostles, was a Jew of Edessa who came to Jerusalem, heard the preaching of John the Forerunner, and became a disciple of the Lord. According to the ancient tradition of the Church, after Pentecost he was sent to Edessa, where he healed the ruler Abgar, preached the Gospel, and established the Church in that city.

Having enlightened many in Mesopotamia, he completed his apostolic labors in peace. He is commemorated on August 21.

8-23.name: Lupus the Martyr
8-23.bio:
St. Lupus was, according to tradition, the faithful servant of the Great Martyr Demetrios of Thessaloniki. Present at his master's martyrdom at the beginning of the fourth century, he reverently kept relics of the saint, through which God worked healings among the faithful of the city.

When this became known he was seized, and confessing Christ openly he was put to death, following his master in martyrdom. He is commemorated on August 23.

8-24.name: Eutyches the Apostle
8-24.bio:
St. Eutyches was a disciple of the apostolic age, remembered by tradition as a follower of St. John the Theologian who also accompanied St. Paul in his labors for the Gospel. Preaching Christ in various lands, he endured imprisonment and torments for the faith.

Though not numbered among the Seventy, he is honored with the title of apostle for his share in their work of evangelization, and he completed his course as a martyr. He is commemorated on August 24.

8-25.name: Return of the Relics of Bartholomew
8-25.desc: Transfer of Relics of Holy Apostle Bartholomew.
8-25.bio:
This feast commemorates the translation of the relics of the Holy Apostle Bartholomew, one of the Twelve, who preached the Gospel in eastern lands and completed his apostolic course as a martyr. According to tradition, his relics, placed in a coffin and cast into the sea by persecutors, were carried by the waves and received with honor by the faithful, coming at last to the island of Lipari.

The Church glorifies God who preserves the relics of His apostles as wellsprings of blessing. The translation is commemorated on August 25, alongside his principal feast on June 11.

8-25.name: Chrysostomos the New of Florina
8-25.desc: St. Chrysostomos the New, Confessor and Metropolitan of Florina, hierarch of the Genuine Orthodox Church.
8-25.bio:
St. Chrysostomos the New, Metropolitan of Florina, was a hierarch and confessor of the twentieth century. A learned and ascetic bishop, he took up the leadership of the Genuine Orthodox Christians of Greece who held to the traditional church calendar, and for this confession he endured deprivation, censure, and exile, bearing all with patience and meekness.

He reposed in 1955, revered by his flock as a confessor of the faith. His memory is honored on August 25, and he is invoked as an intercessor by those who cherish the traditions of the fathers.

8-26.name: Adrian and Natalia
8-26.bio:
Sts. Adrian and Natalia were a married couple of Nicomedia in the time of the persecution of Maximian, at the beginning of the fourth century. Adrian, an imperial official, was so moved by the courage of imprisoned Christians that he confessed Christ and was enrolled among them; his young wife Natalia, secretly a Christian, strengthened him in prison and stood by him through his tortures and martyrdom.

Natalia afterward guarded his memory faithfully and reposed in peace, counted among the confessors. They are commemorated together on August 26 as an image of marriage sanctified by faith.

8-27.name: Poimenas the Great
8-27.desc: Venerable Poimen the Great, desert father.
8-27.bio:
St. Poimen the Great was one of the most renowned of the desert fathers of Egypt, living in the fourth and fifth centuries. With his brothers he took up the monastic life in Sketis, and became a discerning elder to whom monks came from afar for a word of guidance.

More of his sayings are preserved in the Sayings of the Desert Fathers than of any other elder, breathing humility, mercy toward the sinner, and sobriety of soul. His name means shepherd. He reposed at a great age and is commemorated on August 27.

8-27.name: Phanourios
8-27.desc: Holy Great Martyr Phanourios the Newly Revealed of Rhodes.
8-27.bio:
St. Phanourios is a Great Martyr whose icon was discovered on the island of Rhodes in the fourteenth century, showing a young soldier surrounded by scenes of his sufferings for Christ. His name means the one who reveals, and nothing of his life is known beyond what the icon itself testifies: that he endured many tortures and gave his life rather than deny his Lord.

He is beloved throughout the Greek world as the revealer of lost things. According to tradition, the faithful bake a phanouropita, a simple spice cake, in his honor when asking his intercession, sharing it with others in remembrance of his mother.

8-28.name: Moses the Ethiopian
8-28.desc: Venerable Moses the Ethiopian, desert father.
8-28.bio:
St. Moses the Ethiopian was in his youth a slave and then the leader of a band of robbers in Egypt, feared for his strength and violence. Coming to himself, he repented and entered the monastic life in the desert of Sketis, where through long struggle with his former passions he attained deep humility and gentleness, and was found worthy of the priesthood.

He was killed when barbarians attacked the monastery, having refused to lift a weapon in his own defense. A powerful witness that no sinner is beyond repentance, he is commemorated on August 28.

8-29.name: Beheading of John the Baptist
8-29.desc: Beheading of the Holy Glorious Prophet and Forerunner John the Baptist.
8-29.bio:
The Church commemorates on August 29 the martyric death of St. John the Forerunner. Imprisoned by Herod Antipas for rebuking his unlawful union with Herodias, John was beheaded at the request of Herodias, made through her daughter, whose dancing had pleased Herod at his birthday feast. Thus the greatest of the prophets sealed his preaching of repentance with his blood.

The day is kept as a strict fast, in sorrow for the deed and in honor of the Forerunner. The faithful remember him as the friend of the Bridegroom, who according to the hymns of the Church preached the coming of Christ even to those in Hades.

8-30.name: Alexander the Patrician
8-30.bio:
St. Alexander was a martyr of the early Church who confessed Christ before his persecutors and sealed his faith with his blood. The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond his noble standing and his faithful confession unto death.

His memory is kept among the saints of this day, and those who bear the name Alexander honor him in their prayers. He is commemorated on August 30.

8-31.name: Aidan of Lindisfarne
8-31.bio:
St. Aidan was an Irish monk of the monastery of Iona who in the seventh century was sent at the request of King Oswald to evangelize the kingdom of Northumbria in northern England. Consecrated bishop, he made his seat on the island of Lindisfarne, from which he traveled on foot through the countryside, preaching Christ with gentleness, ransoming captives, and giving to the poor whatever he received.

His humility and charity won the hearts of the people, and Lindisfarne became a great center of prayer and mission. He reposed in 651 and is commemorated on August 31.

9-1.name: Beginning of the Church Year
9-1.desc: The Indiction — beginning of the Ecclesiastical New Year.
9-1.bio:
September 1 marks the Indiction, the beginning of the Ecclesiastical New Year. The custom derives from the civil calendar of the Roman Empire, in which the yearly cycle of taxation and public life began in September, and the Church took up this reckoning for her own cycle of feasts.

On this day the Church prays for God's blessing upon the new year, remembering that Christ read in the synagogue at Nazareth the words of Isaiah, "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me... to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord." It is also kept in our time as a day of prayer for the protection of the natural environment.

9-1.name: Simeon Stylites the Elder
9-1.desc: Venerable Symeon Stylites the Elder who stood 36 years on a pillar.
9-1.bio:
St. Simeon Stylites the Elder was a Syrian ascetic of the fifth century who, seeking greater stillness, took up his dwelling on top of a pillar near Antioch. There he stood for many years in prayer and fasting, teaching the crowds who gathered below and reconciling enemies, until his repose in the year 459.

He was the first and most famous of the pillar-dwellers, and his extraordinary endurance made him a wonder of the Christian world even in his lifetime. He is commemorated on September 1, at the opening of the church year.

9-1.name: 40 Holy Virgin Martyrs of Thrace
9-1.desc: The 40 Holy Ascetic Virgin Martyrs of Thrace and their teacher Ammon the Deacon.
9-1.bio:
The 40 Holy Virgins were ascetic women of Thrace who, with their teacher Ammon the Deacon, confessed Christ during the persecution under Licinius in the early fourth century. Refusing to sacrifice to idols, they endured imprisonment and torture with their teacher, and received together the crown of martyrdom at Heraclea in Thrace.

Greek tradition preserves their forty names — among them Ourania, Aspasia, Penelope, Margarita, Erato, Kleio, and Melpomeni — and on September 1 women bearing these names celebrate their name day. The holy virgins and St. Ammon are honored as examples of steadfast faith at the very opening of the church year.

9-2.name: Mamas
9-2.bio:
St. Mamas was a young shepherd of Caesarea in Cappadocia, born to parents who had themselves suffered imprisonment for Christ. Living simply in the hills with his flock, he confessed the faith openly during the persecutions of the third century and endured torture and death rather than deny his Lord.

He has been venerated from ancient times as a protector of shepherds and their flocks, and churches in his honor spread throughout Cappadocia, Cyprus, and Greece. He is commemorated on September 2.

9-3.name: Anthimos of Nicomedia
9-3.bio:
St. Anthimos was Bishop of Nicomedia during the great persecution under Diocletian at the opening of the fourth century. When many of his flock were slain, he shepherded the survivors from hiding, strengthening them by letters and prayer, until he was discovered, confessed Christ before his judges, and was beheaded.

He is honored as a hieromartyr who laid down his life for the flock entrusted to him. He is commemorated on September 3.

9-4.name: Babylas of Antioch
9-4.desc: Holy Hieromartyr Babylas, Patriarch of Antioch.
9-4.bio:
St. Babylas was Bishop of Antioch in the third century, remembered for his boldness in barring an emperor stained with blood from entering the church until he should repent. During the persecution under Decius he was imprisoned for his confession of Christ and died in chains around the year 253.

His relics were greatly honored in Antioch, and his memory endured as an example of a shepherd who feared God more than earthly power. He is commemorated on September 4.

9-5.name: Zacharias the Prophet
9-5.desc: Prophet Zacharias and Elizabeth, parents of John the Baptist.
9-5.bio:
The holy Prophet Zacharias was a priest of the Temple in Jerusalem and the father of St. John the Baptist. The Archangel Gabriel announced to him at the altar of incense that his wife Elizabeth, barren and advanced in years, would bear a son; and at the child's birth Zacharias prophesied concerning the coming salvation of Israel.

Tradition holds that he was slain in the Temple for refusing to betray his son during Herod's slaughter of the infants. With righteous Elizabeth he is commemorated on September 5.

9-6.name: Miracle of Archangel Michael at Chonae
9-6.desc: Miracle of the Archangel Michael at Chonae.
9-6.bio:
This feast commemorates the miracle wrought by the Archangel Michael at Chonae in Asia Minor. According to tradition, pagans sought to destroy a church and healing spring dedicated to the Archangel by turning rivers against it; at the prayer of the devout sacristan Archippos, the Archangel appeared, struck the rock with his staff, and channeled the waters harmlessly into a chasm, preserving the holy place.

The Church keeps the memory of this wonder on September 6, honoring the Archangel Michael as protector of the faithful and captain of the heavenly hosts, whose chief feast with the Archangel Gabriel follows on November 8.

9-7.name: Sozont
9-7.bio:
St. Sozon was a shepherd of Cilicia in Asia Minor who tended his flock in prayer and meditation on the Scriptures. During a time of persecution he confessed Christ boldly at Pompeiopolis, and after enduring torture he gave up his soul to God, receiving the crown of martyrdom.

His memory has been kept from early times, and a church was raised over his relics where the faithful sought healing. He is commemorated on September 7.

9-8.name: Nativity of the Theotokos
9-8.desc: The Nativity of our Most Holy Lady the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary.
9-8.bio:
The Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos, celebrated on September 8, is the first Great Feast of the church year. According to tradition, the righteous Joachim and Anna remained childless into old age, bearing reproach with patience and prayer; God heard them and granted them a daughter, Mary, who was to become the Mother of the Saviour.

Her birth is celebrated as the dawn of salvation, the coming into the world of her through whom the Word of God would take flesh. The feast honors also the faithfulness of her parents, and is a day of joy for all who bear the names Maria and Panagiota.

9-9.name: Joachim and Anne
9-9.desc: Holy and God-Bearing Ancestors Joachim and Anne, parents of the Theotokos.
9-9.bio:
Saints Joachim and Anne were the parents of the Most Holy Theotokos. Righteous and devout, they remained childless into old age, bearing reproach with patience and beseeching God with tears; in answer to their prayer they were granted a daughter, Mary, whom they dedicated to the Lord in His Temple.

The Church honors them as the God-bearing ancestors of Christ, and their names are invoked at the close of every Orthodox service. Their synaxis is kept on September 9, the day after the Nativity of the Theotokos.

9-10.name: Pulcheria
9-10.bio:
St. Pulcheria was a Byzantine empress of the fifth century, sister of the Emperor Theodosius II. She took a vow of virginity, guided the empire with wisdom and piety, and was a steadfast defender of the Orthodox faith, laboring for the Fourth Ecumenical Council at Chalcedon which confessed Christ as true God and true man.

She built churches in honor of the Theotokos in Constantinople and used her rank in the service of the Church and the poor. She is commemorated on September 10.

9-11.name: Theodora of Alexandria
9-11.bio:
St. Theodora of Alexandria lived in the fifth century. Having fallen into sin, she was seized with deep repentance and, disguising herself in men's clothing, entered a monastery under the name of the monk Theodore, where she labored for years in humility, obedience, and secret tears, patiently bearing even false accusation.

Only after her repose was her identity revealed, and the brethren marveled at the depth of her repentance. She is honored as a model of contrition and hidden struggle, and is commemorated on September 11.

9-12.name: Autonomous
9-12.bio:
St. Autonomos was a bishop from Italy who, during the persecution under Diocletian, came to Bithynia in Asia Minor, where he preached the Gospel and brought many pagans to faith in Christ. He was slain by a pagan mob while serving the Divine Liturgy, offering his own life together with the bloodless sacrifice.

He is honored as a hieromartyr whose zeal for the Gospel carried him far from his homeland. He is commemorated on September 12.

9-13.name: Kornelios the Centurion
9-13.bio:
St. Cornelius was a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, a devout man who feared God, gave alms generously, and prayed continually. As the Acts of the Apostles relates, an angel directed him to send for the Apostle Peter, and he and his household became the first Gentiles to be baptized into Christ.

Tradition holds that he afterward labored in the preaching of the Gospel and served the Church as a bishop. He is commemorated on September 13.

9-14.name: Exaltation of the Holy Cross
9-14.desc: The Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross.
9-14.bio:
The Universal Exaltation of the Precious and Life-Giving Cross commemorates the finding of the true Cross of Christ in Jerusalem by St. Helen, mother of St. Constantine the Great, in the fourth century. The Cross was raised aloft by the Patriarch before the people, who bowed down crying out for mercy. The feast also recalls the return of the Cross to Jerusalem from Persian captivity in the seventh century.

Kept on September 14 as a strict fast day in reverence for the Passion, the feast celebrates the Cross as the weapon of victory over death. It is the name day of Stavros and Stavroula.

9-15.name: Nikitas the Great Martyr
9-15.bio:
St. Nikitas the Great Martyr was a Goth living beyond the Danube in the fourth century. Converted to Christ, he confessed the faith boldly among his own people, and when a persecution arose against the Christians of that land he was seized, tortured, and given over to death by fire around the year 372.

His relics were reverently recovered by a friend and became a source of blessing to the faithful. Widely venerated in Greece, where his name means victor, he is commemorated on September 15.

9-16.name: Euphemia the All-Praised (2nd)
9-16.desc: Holy Great Martyr Euphemia the All-Praised of Chalcedon.
9-16.bio:
St. Euphemia the All-Praised was a virgin of Chalcedon who suffered martyrdom during the persecution under Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Refusing to join in pagan sacrifice, she endured many tortures and committed her soul to God, receiving the crown of martyrdom in her native city.

A century and a half later, the Fourth Ecumenical Council met at Chalcedon beside her relics, and the Church honors her as a seal and confirmation of the Orthodox confession. Her chief feast is kept on September 16.

9-17.name: Sophia and Faith, Hope, Love
9-17.desc: Holy Martyrs Faith, Hope, Love and their mother Sophia.
9-17.bio:
St. Sophia was a pious widow of Rome in the second century who raised her three young daughters, Faith, Hope, and Love, in devotion to Christ. During the persecution under the Emperor Hadrian the three girls confessed the faith one after another and were put to death before their mother's eyes, and Sophia, having buried them, soon followed them in death from her grief.

Their names — in Greek Sophia, Pistis, Elpis, and Agapi — embody wisdom and the three great virtues, and they are beloved patrons of countless women who bear them. They are commemorated on September 17.

9-18.name: Eumenios of Gortyna
9-18.bio:
St. Eumenios was Bishop of Gortyna in Crete, a shepherd remembered for his gentleness, his generosity to the poor, and his gift of wonderworking. He defended the Orthodox faith of the Church and ended his days in exile in the Thebaid of Egypt, from whence his relics were returned to his flock in Crete.

He is honored among the holy hierarchs of the Cretan church, and is commemorated on September 18.

9-19.name: Trophimos the Apostle
9-19.bio:
St. Trophimos was an early confessor of Christ who suffered in Asia Minor during the persecutions of the third century, together with his companions Sabbatios and Dorymedon. Refusing to take part in pagan festivity, they confessed the faith before their judges and endured torture and death for the name of Christ.

The three martyrs are honored together as faithful witnesses who preferred the eternal joy of Christ to the passing pleasures of the world. They are commemorated on September 19.

9-20.name: Eustace the Great Martyr
9-20.bio:
St. Eustathios, called Placidas before his baptism, was a Roman general of the second century. According to tradition he was converted while hunting, beholding a vision of the Cross between the antlers of a stag; he was baptized with his wife Theopiste and their two sons, endured the loss of all his possessions and family, and after years of trial was reunited with them.

When he refused to offer pagan sacrifice after a military victory, he and his family were martyred together. He is commemorated on September 20.

9-21.name: Quadratos the Apostle
9-21.bio:
St. Quadratus was an apostle of the early Church who preached the Gospel in Athens and in Magnesia, bringing many to the faith of Christ. Tradition associates him with a written defense of the Christians presented to the emperor, one of the earliest apologies for the faith, and he ended his life as a confessor of Christ.

He is honored among the apostolic men who carried the Gospel through Greece and Asia Minor in the generations after the apostles. He is commemorated on September 21.

9-22.name: Phokas the Gardener (2nd)
9-22.bio:
St. Phokas was a humble gardener of Sinope on the Black Sea who lived by the labor of his hands, sharing his produce with the poor and offering hospitality to travelers. When soldiers were sent to execute him for being a Christian, he received them as guests, and having prepared them supper and dug his own grave, he revealed himself in the morning and met death with peace.

He has been venerated from ancient times as a patron of gardeners and of seafarers. He is commemorated on September 22.

9-23.name: Conception of John the Baptist
9-23.desc: Conception of the Holy Forerunner John the Baptist.
9-23.bio:
On September 23 the Church commemorates the conception of St. John the Forerunner. As the priest Zacharias served in the Temple, the Archangel Gabriel appeared to him at the altar of incense, announcing that his prayer was heard and that his wife Elizabeth, barren and advanced in years, would bear a son who would go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah. Because Zacharias doubted, he was left mute until the child was born.

The feast celebrates the power of God who overcomes barrenness and prepares His forerunner, and it opens the cycle of feasts of the Baptist that runs through the church year.

9-24.name: Thekla Equal-to-the-Apostles
9-24.bio:
St. Thekla of Iconium was converted as a young woman by the preaching of the Apostle Paul. Renouncing her betrothal to follow Christ, she was condemned to fire and to wild beasts, but tradition relates that God preserved her unharmed; she then labored in preaching and prayer, ending her long life in asceticism near Seleucia.

The Church honors her as protomartyr among women and equal-to-the-apostles, first of countless women to embrace the way of virginity for Christ. She is commemorated on September 24.

9-25.name: Euphrosyne of Alexandria (2nd)
9-25.bio:
St. Euphrosyne of Alexandria lived in the fifth century. The daughter of a wealthy and pious father, she fled a marriage arranged for her and, disguising herself in men's clothing, entered a monastery of men under the name Smaragdos, where she lived for many years in fasting, prayer, and perfect obscurity.

Only at the end of her life did she reveal herself to her own father, who had long mourned her and who himself took up the monastic life in her cell. She is commemorated on September 25.

9-26.name: Repose of the Evangelist John the Theologian
9-26.desc: Repose of the Holy Apostle and Evangelist John the Theologian.
9-26.bio:
On September 26 the Church commemorates the repose of St. John the Theologian, the beloved disciple of Christ, who leaned upon the breast of the Lord at the Mystical Supper and stood by His Cross, receiving the Theotokos into his care. He wrote the fourth Gospel, three epistles, and the Revelation, and shepherded the churches of Asia from Ephesus.

Alone among the apostles he was not slain, but reposed in peace at Ephesus in great old age, ceaselessly repeating his teaching: little children, love one another. His memory is kept on September 26.

9-27.name: Kallistratos
9-27.bio:
St. Kallistratos was a Christian soldier who suffered during the persecutions at the turn of the fourth century. Discovered at prayer, he confessed Christ before his commander and was cast into the sea sewn in a sack; delivered unharmed, his courage and deliverance brought forty-nine of his fellow soldiers to believe, and together they received the crown of martyrdom by the sword.

He and his companions are honored as soldiers who exchanged earthly service for the army of Christ. They are commemorated on September 27.

9-28.name: Chariton the Confessor
9-28.bio:
St. Chariton was a Christian of Iconium who confessed Christ under torture during the persecutions of the third century, earning the title of Confessor. Released when the persecution abated, he withdrew to the desert of Judea, where he founded some of the earliest monastic communities of Palestine and guided many souls in the ascetic life.

He is honored as a father of Palestinian monasticism, whose lavras nurtured generations of desert saints. He is commemorated on September 28.

9-29.name: Cyriac the Hermit
9-29.bio:
St. Cyriacus the Hermit was a Palestinian ascetic of the fifth and sixth centuries. Coming to the Holy Land as a young man, he passed his long life in the desert of Judea in the communities founded by the great desert fathers, advancing ever deeper into solitude, fasting, and unceasing prayer, and attaining great old age.

He was a firm defender of the Orthodox faith against the errors of his time, and many sought out his counsel in the wilderness. He is commemorated on September 29.

9-30.name: Gregory of Armenia
9-30.bio:
St. Gregory, the Illuminator of Armenia, brought the Gospel to the Armenian people at the turn of the fourth century. For his confession of Christ he endured long imprisonment in a deep pit, yet through his patience and prayer King Tiridates was converted, and Gregory, consecrated bishop, baptized the king and his people, making Armenia one of the first Christian nations.

He is honored as the apostle and first hierarch of the Armenian church, and his memory is kept throughout the Orthodox world on September 30.

10-1.name: Protection of the Theotokos
10-1.desc: The Protection of Our Most Holy Lady the Theotokos (celebrated primarily in Russian and Serbian Orthodox Church).
10-1.bio:
The feast of the Protection, or Pokrov, commemorates a vision granted in the tenth century at the Blachernae church in Constantinople, where the robe of the Theotokos was kept. During an all-night vigil, St. Andrew the Fool-for-Christ beheld the Mother of God standing above the people, praying with tears and spreading her veil over the faithful as a shelter.

The feast, kept on October 1 and beloved especially in the Russian and Serbian churches, celebrates the unceasing intercession of the Theotokos, who covers the Christian people with her protection in every trial.

10-2.name: Cyprian and Justina
10-2.bio:
St. Cyprian was a famed sorcerer of Antioch who was hired to bend the Christian virgin Justina to an unwanted suitor. Every art of his magic was shattered against her prayer and the sign of the Cross, and Cyprian, recognizing a power greater than all his demons, burned his books, was baptized, and in time became a bishop of the Church.

During the persecution under Diocletian, Cyprian and Justina were arrested, tortured, and beheaded together. They are invoked by the faithful against the works of magic and are commemorated on October 2.

10-3.name: Dionysios the Areopagite
10-3.desc: Holy Hieromartyr Dionysios the Areopagite, first Bishop of Athens.
10-3.bio:
St. Dionysios the Areopagite was an Athenian of the first century, a member of the court of the Areopagus, converted when the Apostle Paul preached in Athens of the God whom the city honored without knowing. According to tradition he became the first Bishop of Athens and ended his life as a martyr.

He is the patron saint of the city of Athens, where his memory has been honored from ancient times. His feast is kept on October 3, a beloved name day for those called Dionysios and Dionysia.

10-4.name: Hierotheus of Athens
10-4.desc: Bishop Hierotheos, first Bishop of Athens.
10-4.bio:
St. Hierotheos was an Athenian of the apostolic age, converted by the preaching of the Apostle Paul and made a bishop of Athens. Tradition remembers him as a man of deep divine wisdom, the teacher and companion of St. Dionysios the Areopagite, and relates that he was present with the apostles at the Dormition of the Theotokos, where his hymnody moved all who heard him.

He is honored among the first hierarchs of Greece, and is commemorated on October 4.

10-5.name: Charitine
10-5.bio:
St. Charitina was a young Christian woman who suffered martyrdom during the persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century. An orphan raised by a pious guardian, she lived in prayer and purity, and when she was denounced as a Christian she confessed Christ boldly, enduring cruel tortures until she gave her soul to God.

She is numbered among the holy virgin martyrs whose steadfastness put their persecutors to shame. She is commemorated on October 5.

10-6.name: Thomas the Apostle
10-6.bio:
St. Thomas, called the Twin, was one of the Twelve Apostles. Absent when the risen Christ first appeared to the disciples, he said he would not believe unless he touched the wounds of the Lord; eight days later Christ invited him to do so, and Thomas confessed Him as Lord and God — the clearest confession of the divinity of Christ in the Gospels.

According to tradition Thomas carried the Gospel east as far as India, where ancient Christian communities trace their origin to his preaching, and where he died a martyr. He is commemorated on October 6 and on the first Sunday after Pascha.

10-7.name: Sergios and Vakchos
10-7.bio:
Saints Sergius and Bacchus were high-ranking officers in the Roman army at the end of the third century, secretly Christians and beloved of the emperor. When their faith was discovered they refused to sacrifice to the idols; stripped of their rank, they were paraded in mockery and cruelly tortured. Bacchus died under the blows, and Sergius was afterward beheaded in Syria.

The city of Resafa, where Sergius suffered, became a great center of pilgrimage bearing his name. The two friends and fellow soldiers of Christ are commemorated together on October 7.

10-8.name: Pelagia
10-8.bio:
St. Pelagia was a celebrated actress of Antioch, renowned for her beauty and wealth, who was brought to compunction by the preaching of a holy bishop. She was baptized, gave her riches to the poor, and departed secretly to Jerusalem, where she lived in a cell on the Mount of Olives in strict asceticism, unknown to all until her repose.

She is honored as a model of true repentance, showing that no life is beyond the reach of the mercy of God. She is commemorated on October 8.

10-9.name: James the Apostle
10-9.desc: Holy Apostle James, Brother of the Lord.
10-9.bio:
St. James the Brother of the Lord was the son of righteous Joseph and is called Adelphotheos, kinsman of Christ according to the flesh. He became the first Bishop of Jerusalem, presided at the apostolic council described in Acts, and wrote the catholic epistle that bears his name; his righteousness was such that he was called the Just even by those outside the Church.

According to tradition he was cast down from the pinnacle of the Temple for his confession of Christ and so received a martyr's death. The ancient Liturgy of St. James bears his name, and he is commemorated on October 9.

10-9.name: James the Apostle of Alphaeus
10-9.desc: Holy Apostle James son of Alpheus.
10-9.bio:
St. James the son of Alphaeus was one of the Twelve Apostles chosen by the Lord, named in each of the Gospel lists of the Twelve. After Pentecost he went forth, as the apostles did, to preach the Gospel among the nations, and tradition relates that he ended his labors as a martyr for Christ.

The synaxaria preserve little of the details of his journeys, but the Church honors him among the foundational Twelve upon whose preaching she is built. He is commemorated on October 9.

10-10.name: Eulampios and Eulampia
10-10.bio:
Saints Eulampios and Eulampia were brother and sister, Christians of Nicomedia during the persecution under the Emperor Maximian at the beginning of the fourth century. When Eulampios was seized and tortured for confessing Christ, his sister Eulampia openly declared her own faith so that she might share his sufferings, and together they endured torment and received the crown of martyrdom.

Their courage moved many who witnessed it to believe in Christ. The two siblings are commemorated together on October 10.

10-11.name: Philip the Apostle (Deacon)
10-11.desc: Holy Apostle Philip of the Seven Deacons.
10-11.bio:
St. Philip was one of the seven deacons chosen by the apostles to serve the early Church in Jerusalem, as the Acts of the Apostles relates. Full of the Holy Spirit, he preached Christ in Samaria with great power, and on the desert road he baptized the Ethiopian eunuch, opening the Gospel to the nations.

Tradition relates that he continued his apostolic labors and served the Church as a bishop in Asia Minor, where his daughters also were known for the gift of prophecy. He is commemorated on October 11.

10-12.name: Probus and Tarachos
10-12.desc: Holy Martyrs Probus, Tarachos, and Andronicus.
10-12.bio:
Saints Probus and Tarachos, together with Andronicus, were Christians of Cilicia who suffered during the persecution under Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. Differing in age and station, they were united in their confession; brought repeatedly before the judges, they endured prolonged tortures with astonishing endurance and were finally put to death for Christ.

The faithful reverently gathered their relics, and the three are honored together as steadfast athletes of the faith. They are commemorated on October 12.

10-13.name: Carpus and Papylus
10-13.bio:
Saints Carpus and Papylus suffered for Christ during the persecutions of the third century in Asia Minor. Carpus, a bishop, and Papylus, a deacon known for his care of the sick, refused to offer pagan sacrifice; with their companions they endured torture with joy and received the crown of martyrdom at Pergamum.

Their witness, preserved in some of the most ancient martyr accounts of the Church, strengthened the faithful of Asia Minor in a time of trial. They are commemorated on October 13.

10-14.name: Nazarios, Gervase, Prothase
10-14.desc: Holy Martyrs Nazarius, Gervase, and Prothasius.
10-14.bio:
Saints Nazarius, Gervasius, and Protasius, with their companion Celsius, were martyrs of the early Church in Italy, put to death for Christ at Milan in the first age of persecution. The synaxaria relate that Nazarius preached the Gospel with apostolic zeal, and that the young Celsius followed him even unto death.

Their relics were found centuries later in Milan in the days of St. Ambrose, to the great joy of the Church, and their veneration spread through both East and West. They are commemorated on October 14.

10-15.name: Lucian of Antioch
10-15.bio:
St. Lucian was a priest of Antioch, renowned as a scholar of the Holy Scriptures, who labored over the sacred text and taught many disciples in the school of Antioch. During the persecution at the beginning of the fourth century he was arrested and taken to Nicomedia, where after a bold defense of the faith he died in prison for Christ around the year 312.

He is honored as a hieromartyr and teacher whose love for the Scriptures marked the whole church of Antioch. He is commemorated on October 15.

10-16.name: Longinus the Centurion
10-16.desc: Holy Martyr Longinus the Centurion who pierced Christ's side.
10-16.bio:
St. Longinus was the centurion who stood guard at the Cross of Christ and, beholding the darkness and the earthquake, confessed: truly this was the Son of God. Tradition holds that he was also among the guards at the tomb, and that having become a believer he left the army and preached Christ in his native Cappadocia.

For this confession he was beheaded, sealing with his blood the faith he first proclaimed on Golgotha. He is commemorated on October 16.

10-17.name: Osee the Prophet
10-17.bio:
The holy Prophet Hosea was one of the twelve minor prophets, who prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ. Through the image of his own sorrowful marriage he proclaimed the unfailing love of God for His unfaithful people, calling Israel to repentance with words of both judgment and tenderness.

His prophecy, I desire mercy and not sacrifice, was taken up by the Lord Himself in the Gospels. He is commemorated on October 17.

10-18.name: Luke the Evangelist
10-18.bio:
St. Luke the Evangelist was a physician of Antioch and a companion of the Apostle Paul in his missionary labors. He wrote the third Gospel, which preserves the fullest account of the Nativity and the parables of divine mercy, and the Acts of the Apostles, the history of the Church's first years.

Tradition honors him also as the first iconographer, who painted the image of the Most Holy Theotokos, and relates that he served the Gospel into old age in Greece. The beloved physician and evangelist is commemorated on October 18.

10-19.name: Joel the Prophet
10-19.bio:
The holy Prophet Joel was one of the twelve minor prophets, who prophesied in the kingdom of Judah. In a time of devastation he called the people to fasting and heartfelt repentance, and he foretold the day when God would pour out His Spirit upon all flesh.

That prophecy was fulfilled at Pentecost, when the Apostle Peter proclaimed Joel's words to the crowds in Jerusalem at the descent of the Holy Spirit. He is commemorated on October 19.

10-20.name: Artemon of Seleucia
10-20.bio:
