The holy Great Martyr Artemios was a distinguished military commander of the fourth century who served under St. Constantine the Great and his successors. When the Emperor Julian the Apostate sought to restore paganism, Artemios rebuked him openly for his persecution of the Christians; for this he was stripped of his rank, cruelly tortured, and beheaded at Antioch in the year 362.

His relics were brought to Constantinople, where many miracles of healing were wrought, and he has long been invoked by the faithful for healing of bodily ailments. He is commemorated on October 20.

10-21.name: Hilarion the Great
10-21.desc: Venerable Hilarion the Great, father of Palestinian monasticism.
10-21.bio:
St. Hilarion the Great was born near Gaza in Palestine at the end of the third century. Inspired by the example of St. Anthony the Great, whom he visited in the Egyptian desert, he took up the ascetic life in his homeland and became the father of monasticism in Palestine, drawing many disciples by his fasting, humility, and gift of wonderworking.

Fleeing the fame of his miracles, he wandered from land to land seeking stillness, and reposed in Cyprus in old age. He is commemorated on October 21.

10-22.name: Abercius of Hieropolis
10-22.bio:
St. Abercius was Bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia in the second century, called Equal-to-the-Apostles for his missionary zeal. He overthrew the idols of his city, brought multitudes to faith in Christ by his preaching and healings, and journeyed as far as Rome and the lands of the East, everywhere confirming the churches.

His famous epitaph, composed by the saint himself, speaks in veiled language of the Eucharist and the universal Church, and stands among the most precious monuments of early Christianity. He is commemorated on October 22.

10-24.name: Arethas of Najran
10-24.bio:
St. Arethas was the chief of the Christians of Najran in southern Arabia in the sixth century. When a persecutor seized the city and demanded that its people renounce Christ, the aged Arethas strengthened his fellow Christians in the faith, and with a great multitude of men, women, and children he was put to death around the year 523.

The blood of the martyrs of Najran bore witness to Christ in the Arabian peninsula, and their memory was honored throughout the Christian East. St. Arethas and those with him are commemorated on October 24.

10-25.name: Tabitha
10-25.bio:
St. Tabitha, called Dorcas in Greek, was a disciple of Christ living at Joppa in the days of the apostles. The Acts of the Apostles describes her as full of good works and almsgiving, sewing garments for the widows and the poor; when she fell sick and died, the Apostle Peter was summoned, and by his prayer God raised her from the dead.

Her restoration to life brought many in Joppa to believe in the Lord, and she remains a model of practical, quiet charity. She is commemorated on October 25.

10-26.name: Demetrios the Great Martyr
10-26.desc: Great Martyr Demetrios of Thessaloniki, Myrrh-Streamer.
10-26.bio:
St. Demetrios the Great Martyr and Myrrh-Streamer was a young nobleman and military commander of Thessaloniki, martyred under the Emperor Maximian at the beginning of the fourth century. Imprisoned for openly teaching the faith, he blessed the young Nestor, who defeated the gladiator Lyaios in the arena; for this Demetrios was run through with spears in his prison.

From his relics, according to tradition, fragrant myrrh flowed, and he is honored as the great protector of Thessaloniki, where his basilica has stood for fifteen centuries. His feast on October 26 is one of the great celebrations of northern Greece.

10-27.name: Nestor the Martyr
10-27.bio:
St. Nestor was a young Christian of Thessaloniki, a disciple of the Great Martyr Demetrios. When the gladiator Lyaios was slaying challengers to the delight of the Emperor Maximian, Nestor received the blessing of the imprisoned Demetrios, entered the arena with the prayer, God of Demetrios, help me, and overthrew the boastful champion.

For this the enraged emperor ordered Nestor put to death, and he received the crown of martyrdom the day after his teacher. He is commemorated on October 27, in the afterglow of the feast of St. Demetrios.

10-28.name: Terentios and companions
10-28.bio:
St. Terentios suffered for Christ in the early centuries of persecution together with his wife Neonilla and their children. Refusing to deny the faith in which they had raised their household, the whole family confessed Christ together and together received the crown of martyrdom.

They are honored as an image of the Christian family united in faith even unto death, parents and children strengthening one another in their confession. They are commemorated on October 28.

10-29.name: Anastasios the Younger
10-29.bio:
St. Anastasios is remembered as a hierarch who served the Church of Constantinople, of whom the synaxaria preserve little beyond his faithful service and holy repose.

The Church honors in him, as in many shepherds whose deeds are known fully to God alone, the quiet faithfulness of those who kept the flock of Christ in difficult times. He is commemorated on October 29.

10-30.name: Zenobios and Zenobia
10-30.bio:
Saints Zenobios and Zenobia were brother and sister from Cilicia in Asia Minor. Zenobios, a physician who healed the sick without payment in the name of Christ, became a bishop of the Church; during the persecution under Diocletian he was arrested, and Zenobia freely joined her brother so that she might share his confession and his sufferings.

Together they endured torture and were beheaded, receiving the crown of martyrdom. The two siblings are commemorated together on October 30.

10-31.name: Stachys the Apostle
10-31.desc: Holy Apostle Stachys, first Bishop of Byzantium.
10-31.bio:
St. Stachys was one of the Seventy Apostles, greeted by name by the Apostle Paul in his epistle to the Romans. Tradition relates that he was ordained by the Apostle Andrew as the first Bishop of Byzantium, the city that would one day become Constantinople, where he shepherded the young Christian community and labored in the preaching of the Gospel.

He is honored as the first in the long line of hierarchs of the imperial city. Together with the apostles Apelles, Amplias, Urban, Narcissus, and Aristobulus of the Seventy, he is commemorated on October 31.

11-1.name: Kosmas and Damian (Asian)
11-1.desc: Holy Unmercenary Physicians Cosmas and Damian of Asia.
11-1.bio:
Saints Kosmas and Damian of Asia Minor were brothers and physicians, raised in the faith by their pious mother Theodota. They treated the sick without ever accepting payment, asking only that those they healed believe in Christ, and for this the Church calls them Unmercenaries. They reposed in peace after lives given wholly to God and neighbor.

They are the first of several pairs of unmercenary physicians named Kosmas and Damian honored in the church year, and they are invoked by the sick and by those in the healing professions. They are commemorated on November 1.

11-2.name: Akindynos and companions
11-2.desc: Holy Martyrs Acindynus, Pigasius and companions.
11-2.bio:
The holy martyrs Akindynos, Pegasios, Aphthonios, Elpidophoros, and Anempodistos were Christians of Persia who suffered in the fourth century, during a fierce persecution of the Church in that land. Refusing to deny Christ, they endured many torments and were put to death, and their steadfastness drew others to the faith.

The Church honors them as a company of confessors whose courage strengthened the persecuted Christians of Persia. They are commemorated on November 2.

11-3.name: Akepsimas of Persia
11-3.bio:
The holy hieromartyr Akepsimas was a bishop in Persia who suffered in the great persecution of the fourth century. Though advanced in years, he endured imprisonment and torture rather than worship the sun as his persecutors demanded, and he was put to death for his confession of Christ, together with the priest Joseph and the deacon Aeithalas.

The Church remembers him as a faithful shepherd who sealed a long life of service with martyrdom. He is commemorated on November 3.

11-4.name: Ioannikios the Great
11-4.bio:
Venerable Ioannikios the Great was born in Bithynia in the eighth century and served for years as a soldier before leaving the world for the monastic life on Mount Olympus in Asia Minor. There he lived in great asceticism and prayer, receiving gifts of prophecy and wonderworking, and he stood with the venerators of the holy icons in the troubled years of iconoclasm.

He reposed in peace in old age, revered by monks and hierarchs alike as one of the great ascetics of his time. He is commemorated on November 4.

11-5.name: Galaktion and Episteme
11-5.bio:
Saints Galaktion and Episteme were a young married couple of Emesa in Syria who, according to tradition, agreed to preserve chastity and gave themselves to the ascetic life, each entering a monastic community. When persecution arose, Galaktion was seized for his faith, and Episteme freely joined him in confessing Christ; together they endured torture and were put to death.

The Church honors them as a pair united first in marriage and finally in martyrdom. They are commemorated on November 5.

11-6.name: Paul the Confessor
11-6.bio:
St. Paul the Confessor was Archbishop of Constantinople in the fourth century, in the years when the Arian heresy was upheld by the powerful. A firm defender of the Nicene faith, he was driven from his see repeatedly by Arian opponents and finally exiled to a remote place, where he was put to death by those who hated his orthodoxy.

The Church honors him as a confessor who preferred exile and death to the betrayal of the true faith. He is commemorated on November 6.

11-7.name: Lazaros of Mount Galesion
11-7.bio:
Venerable Lazaros of Mount Galesion was an ascetic of the eleventh century who, after years of pilgrimage and monastic labor in the Holy Land, settled on Mount Galesion near Ephesus. There he took up the harsh discipline of the stylites, living upon a pillar in prayer and fasting, and a community of monks gathered around him under his direction.

Renowned for discernment and compassion toward all who sought him out, he reposed in peace. He is commemorated on November 7.

11-8.name: Synaxis of Archangels Michael and Gabriel
11-8.desc: Synaxis of the Chief Incorporeal Powers — Archangels Michael and Gabriel.
11-8.bio:
On November 8 the Church celebrates the Synaxis of the Archangels Michael and Gabriel together with all the Bodiless Powers of heaven. Michael, whose name asks Who is like God, is honored as the chief commander of the heavenly hosts who stood firm when the rebellious angels fell; Gabriel is the messenger who announced the Incarnation to the Theotokos.

The feast confesses the ministry of the angels, created spirits who glorify God and are sent for the aid of the faithful. It is one of the great name days of the Greek world, celebrated by those named Michael, Gabriel, and Angelos.

11-9.name: Onesiphoros the Apostle
11-9.bio:
The holy apostle Onesiphoros, one of the Seventy, is remembered with honor by the Apostle Paul in his second epistle to Timothy. When Paul was imprisoned in Rome, Onesiphoros sought him out diligently and refreshed him, unashamed of the Apostle's chains, and Paul prayed that the Lord grant mercy to his whole household.

Tradition holds that he continued in apostolic labors and ended his life as a martyr for Christ. He is commemorated on November 9.

11-9.name: Nektarios of Aegina
11-9.desc: St. Nektarios of Aegina, Metropolitan of Pentapolis, wonderworker.
11-9.bio:
St. Nektarios of Aegina, Metropolitan of Pentapolis, is one of the most beloved saints of modern Greece. Born in Selybria of Thrace in 1846, he served the Church with great humility and was slandered and unjustly removed from his see in Egypt, bearing the injustice without bitterness. He later taught in Athens and founded the Holy Trinity Convent on the island of Aegina, where he reposed in 1920.

Countless healings have been attributed to his intercession, and he is invoked especially by those suffering from cancer and serious illness. He was glorified as a saint by the Ecumenical Patriarchate in 1961, and his feast is a major name day for those named Nektarios and Nektaria.

11-10.name: Erastos the Apostle
11-10.bio:
The holy apostle Erastos, one of the Seventy, is named by the Apostle Paul in his epistle to the Romans as the treasurer of the city of Corinth. A companion of Paul in the work of the Gospel, he served the growing Church with the same faithfulness he had shown in civic office.

Tradition remembers him as continuing in ministry among the first generation of Christians, laboring for the spread of the faith. He is commemorated on November 10.

11-11.name: Victor and Stephanida
11-11.bio:
The holy martyr Victor was a Christian soldier who suffered for Christ in the second century, refusing to sacrifice to idols and enduring cruel tortures with unshaken faith. Stephanida, the young wife of another soldier, saw his endurance, confessed Christ openly, and was put to death with him.

The Church honors them together as witnesses whose courage under torment revealed the power of grace. They are commemorated on November 11.

11-12.name: John the Merciful
11-12.bio:
St. John the Merciful, a native of Cyprus, became Patriarch of Alexandria in the early seventh century. He earned his title by boundless almsgiving: he called the poor his masters, kept a register of the needy of the city, and poured out the wealth of the Church in feeding, clothing, and ransoming all who came to him, trusting that God would never be outgiven.

He reposed in peace in his homeland of Cyprus, and his example remains the Church's great icon of mercy toward the poor. He is commemorated on November 12.

11-13.name: John Chrysostom (repose)
11-13.bio:
St. John Chrysostom, the golden-mouthed preacher, was Archbishop of Constantinople at the turn of the fifth century. The greatest homilist of the Church, he expounded the Scriptures to his flock, defended the poor, and rebuked the powerful without fear, for which he was twice driven into exile; he died on the road in exile, with the words Glory to God for all things on his lips.

The Divine Liturgy most often celebrated in the Orthodox Church bears his name, and he is counted among the Three Holy Hierarchs. His repose is commemorated on November 13.

11-14.name: Philip the Apostle
11-14.desc: Holy Apostle Philip, one of the Twelve.
11-14.bio:
The holy apostle Philip, one of the Twelve, was from Bethsaida of Galilee, the city of Peter and Andrew. Called by the Lord Himself, he brought Nathanael to Christ with the words Come and see, and in the Gospel of John he asks the Lord to show the disciples the Father. After Pentecost he preached the Gospel in Asia Minor and, according to tradition, ended his life as a martyr at Hierapolis.

The Nativity Fast begins the day after his feast, which is why it is called St. Philip's Fast in many lands. He is commemorated on November 14.

11-15.name: Gurias and Samonas
11-15.desc: Holy Martyrs Gourias, Samonas and Abibus.
11-15.bio:
The holy confessors Gurias and Samonas were Christians of Edessa in Mesopotamia who suffered for Christ in the persecutions of the early fourth century, enduring imprisonment and torture before being put to death. The deacon Abibus, martyred in the same city some years later, is honored with them.

The three are venerated in Edessa and throughout the Church as protectors of the wronged, and many faithful have sought their intercession in distress. They are commemorated on November 15.

11-16.name: Matthew the Evangelist
11-16.bio:
The holy apostle and evangelist Matthew was a tax collector at Capernaum when the Lord called him with the words Follow me; he rose at once, left everything, and made a feast for Christ in his house. One of the Twelve, he wrote the first of the four Gospels, setting forth Christ as the fulfillment of the Law and the Prophets.

After Pentecost he preached the Gospel to many peoples and, according to tradition, ended his life in martyrdom. He is commemorated on November 16.

11-17.name: Gregory the Wonderworker
11-17.desc: Bishop Gregory the Wonderworker of Neocaesarea.
11-17.bio:
St. Gregory the Wonderworker was Bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus in the third century. A student of philosophy who was won to Christ, he received the episcopate of a city with only a handful of Christians; through his preaching and the many miracles God worked through him, it is said that at his death only a handful of pagans remained.

He is one of the earliest saints to bear the title Wonderworker, and the Fathers of Cappadocia honored his memory and his teaching. He is commemorated on November 17.

11-18.name: Plato of Ancyra
11-18.bio:
The holy martyr Plato was a young Christian of Ancyra in Galatia who suffered in the persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century. Brought before the governor, he refused every inducement to deny Christ, answered his judges with boldness and wisdom, and after enduring cruel tortures was beheaded.

The Church remembers him as a fearless young confessor whose witness strengthened the faithful of his city. He is commemorated on November 18.

11-19.name: Abdias the Prophet
11-19.bio:
The holy prophet Abdias, called Obadiah in the Hebrew Scriptures, is one of the twelve minor prophets, and his book is the shortest in the Old Testament. In it he pronounces the judgment of God upon Edom for its pride and its violence against Israel, and he foretells the day of the Lord and the deliverance that shall be upon Mount Zion.

The Church honors him among the prophets who prepared the way for the coming of Christ. He is commemorated on November 19.

11-20.name: Proclus the Martyr
11-20.bio:
The holy martyrs Proclus and Hilarius suffered for Christ in the early centuries of the Church, during the Roman persecutions. Tradition relates that Proclus was seized first and endured torture with steadfastness, and that his witness moved his kinsman Hilarius to confess Christ openly; both were put to death for the faith.

The synaxaria preserve little more than their faithful confession, which the Church treasures as a seed of the Gospel. They are commemorated on November 20.

11-21.name: Entry of the Theotokos into the Temple
11-21.desc: The Entry of our Most Holy Lady the Theotokos into the Temple.
11-21.bio:
The Entry of the Theotokos into the Temple, kept on November 21, commemorates the day the child Mary, at the age of three, was brought by her parents Joachim and Anna to the Temple in Jerusalem in fulfillment of their vow. According to tradition she was received by the priest Zacharias and dwelt in the Temple, nourished in prayer and prepared to become the living temple of God.

The feast celebrates the dedication of the Mother of God wholly to the Lord from childhood. Falling near the beginning of the Nativity Fast, it points ahead to the mystery of the Incarnation.

11-22.name: Philemon the Apostle
11-22.bio:
The holy apostle Philemon, one of the Seventy, was a Christian of Colossae and the recipient of the Apostle Paul's epistle that bears his name, in which Paul pleads for the runaway slave Onesimus as for a beloved brother. His household was a gathering place for the church of his city.

Tradition holds that he served the Gospel in Asia Minor and ended his life as a martyr, together with his wife Apphia. He is commemorated on November 22.

11-23.name: Amphilochios of Iconium
11-23.bio:
St. Amphilochios was Bishop of Iconium in the fourth century, a kinsman and friend of the great Cappadocian Fathers; St. Basil the Great addressed to him important letters on the canons and dedicated to him his treatise on the Holy Spirit. He labored against the Arian heresy and took part in the Second Ecumenical Council at Constantinople.

A wise shepherd and defender of the divinity of the Son and the Spirit, he reposed in peace in old age. He is commemorated on November 23.

11-24.name: Catherine the Great Martyr
11-24.bio:
St. Catherine the Great Martyr was a noble and brilliantly educated maiden of Alexandria, martyred at the beginning of the fourth century. According to tradition, she confessed Christ before the emperor and bested in debate the philosophers gathered to refute her, leading many to the faith. After torture on the wheel, which was broken by grace, she was beheaded.

Her relics rest at the great monastery of Sinai that bears her name. She is honored as a patroness of learning and students, and her feast, kept on November 24 in some traditions and November 25 in others, is a cherished name day for Katerina.

11-25.name: Clement of Rome
11-25.desc: Pope Clement I of Rome, martyr.
11-25.bio:
St. Clement was Bishop of Rome at the end of the first century, a man of the apostolic generation whom tradition associates with the companions of the Apostles Peter and Paul. His epistle to the Corinthians, written to heal division in that church, is among the most precious writings of the early Church. Exiled for the faith to the region of the Crimea, he labored among the faithful there and was martyred by drowning.

The Church honors him as an apostolic father and hieromartyr whose words still teach concord and humility. He is commemorated on November 25.

11-26.name: Alypios Stylites
11-26.bio:
Venerable Alypios the Stylite was an ascetic of Paphlagonia in Asia Minor who embraced the rare and severe discipline of the pillar saints, standing upon a column in unceasing prayer, exposed to heat and frost, for many decades. From his pillar he taught and consoled the many who came to him, and monastic communities gathered nearby under his care.

He reposed in extreme old age, having endured his ascetic struggle to the end even when his body failed. He is commemorated on November 26.

11-27.name: James the Persian
11-27.bio:
The great martyr James the Persian was a Christian noble at the Persian court in the fifth century who, to please the king, denied Christ. Rebuked by the grief of his mother and his wife, he came to himself, repented, and confessed his faith before the king, for which he was condemned to a slow death by dismemberment; he endured it with prayer, and for this he is called the Cut-to-Pieces.

His repentance and endurance have made him one of the most venerated martyrs of the East. He is commemorated on November 27.

11-28.name: Stephen the Younger
11-28.bio:
The holy monk-martyr Stephen the Younger was an ascetic of Mount Auxentios near Constantinople in the eighth century, during the persecution of the holy icons. A monk from his youth and a guide to many, he refused to subscribe to the iconoclast council and boldly defended the veneration of the icons before the emperor himself; for this he was imprisoned, and he was finally killed by a mob in the streets of the capital.

He is honored as the foremost martyr of the iconoclast persecution. He is commemorated on November 28.

11-29.name: Paramon and Philomenus
11-29.bio:
The holy martyrs Paramon and Philomenus suffered for Christ in the third century, during the Roman persecutions. Tradition relates that Paramon, seeing a multitude of Christians being tortured for refusing to sacrifice to idols, openly confessed Christ and was put to death with them; Philomenus likewise sealed his confession with his blood.

The synaxaria preserve little beyond their faithful witness, which the Church holds in honor among the martyrs of that age. They are commemorated on November 29.

11-30.name: Andrew the First-Called
11-30.desc: Holy First-Called Apostle Andrew, patron of Greece, Russia, and Scotland.
11-30.bio:
St. Andrew, the First-Called of the Apostles, was a fisherman of Bethsaida and first a disciple of St. John the Forerunner. When the Baptist pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, Andrew followed Him at once and brought his brother Simon Peter to the Lord. After Pentecost, according to tradition, he preached the Gospel around the Black Sea and in Greece, and was martyred at Patras on a cross in the form of an X.

He is honored as patron of Greece and of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, whose first bishop tradition names him. His feast is kept on November 30.

12-1.name: Nahum the Prophet
12-1.bio:
The holy prophet Nahum is one of the twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament. He prophesied the fall of Nineveh, the proud capital of Assyria, declaring that the Lord is slow to anger and great in power, a stronghold in the day of trouble to those who trust in Him, and that the oppressor's city would not rise again.

The Church honors him among the prophets whose words prepared Israel for the justice and mercy of God revealed in Christ. He is commemorated on December 1.

12-2.name: Habakkuk the Prophet
12-2.bio:
The holy prophet Habakkuk is one of the twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament. Troubled by the prosperity of the wicked, he questioned God and stood upon his watch to await the answer, receiving the word that the righteous shall live by his faith. His prayer, the canticle beginning Lord, I have heard Thy report and was afraid, is sung in the Church as one of the biblical odes of matins.

The Church honors him as a prophet who foresaw the coming of the Lord for the salvation of His people. He is commemorated on December 2.

12-3.name: Zephaniah the Prophet
12-3.bio:
The holy prophet Zephaniah, one of the twelve minor prophets, prophesied in the kingdom of Judah in the days of King Josiah, before the Babylonian captivity. He proclaimed the great day of the Lord, calling the people to seek righteousness and humility, and he foretold that a meek and lowly remnant would trust in the name of the Lord and rejoice in His salvation.

The Church honors him among the prophets whose words point ahead to the joy of the Messiah's coming. He is commemorated on December 3.

12-4.name: Barbara the Great Martyr
12-4.desc: Great Martyr Barbara of Heliopolis, patron against sudden death.
12-4.bio:
St. Barbara the Great Martyr lived in the late third century. According to tradition, she was the daughter of a wealthy pagan, Dioskoros, who confined her in a tower; coming to faith in Christ, she confessed Him openly, and after cruel tortures she was put to death by her own father, upon whom judgment swiftly fell.

She is invoked as a protector against sudden and unprepared death, and by long tradition is the patroness of those who work with fire and explosives, including miners and artillerymen. Her feast on December 4 is a beloved name day for Barbara and Varvara.

12-5.name: Savvas the Sanctified
12-5.desc: Venerable Sabas the Sanctified, founder of the Great Lavra near Jerusalem.
12-5.bio:
Venerable Savvas the Sanctified, born in Cappadocia in the fifth century, entered the monastic life as a boy and became one of the great fathers of the Judean desert. He founded the Great Lavra near Jerusalem, which bears his name to this day, and gathered thousands of monks under his guidance, while defending the Orthodox faith of the Council of Chalcedon.

The liturgical order long followed throughout the Orthodox Church, the Typikon of St. Savvas, is linked to his monastery. He reposed in peace in old age and is commemorated on December 5.

12-6.name: Nicholas the Wonderworker
12-6.desc: Archbishop of Myra in Lycia, the Wonderworker, patron of sailors, children, and travellers.
12-6.bio:
St. Nicholas the Wonderworker, Archbishop of Myra in Lycia, lived in the fourth century and is one of the most beloved saints of the Church. Renowned for secret almsgiving — according to tradition he saved three daughters of a poor man from ruin by gifts of gold given at night — he was a defender of the innocent and of the true faith in the age of the First Ecumenical Council.

He is the patron of sailors and travelers, of children, and of countless churches and towns across the Orthodox world, and his relics rest in Bari in Italy. His feast is kept on December 6.

12-7.name: Ambrose of Milan
12-7.desc: Archbishop of Milan, one of the four great Latin Fathers.
12-7.bio:
St. Ambrose was Archbishop of Milan in the fourth century and one of the great Fathers of the Western Church. Governor of the region when a disputed episcopal election threatened the city with strife, he was acclaimed bishop by the people while still a catechumen; he gave his wealth to the poor, defended the Nicene faith against Arianism, and did not fear to call even emperors to repentance. His preaching helped bring Blessed Augustine to conversion.

A teacher and hymnographer whose writings nourished East and West alike, he reposed in peace. He is commemorated on December 7.

12-8.name: Patapios
12-8.bio:
Venerable Patapios was born in Thebes of Egypt and embraced the ascetic life in the desert from his youth. Fleeing the fame that his holiness drew, he came to Constantinople, where he lived in stillness and prayer, and many were healed through his intercession; the Church's hymns remember him especially as a healer of the sick.

His relics are treasured at the monastery that bears his name near Loutraki in Greece, where the faithful come in great numbers to venerate him. He is commemorated on December 8.

12-9.name: Conception of the Theotokos by Anne
12-9.desc: Conception of the Most Holy Theotokos by the Righteous Anna.
12-9.bio:
On December 9 the Church commemorates the conception of the Most Holy Theotokos by the righteous Anna. Childless for many years, Joachim and Anna prayed with tears, and according to tradition an angel announced to each of them that God would grant them a child who would be spoken of in all the world. Anna conceived and bore Mary, the future Mother of God.

The feast celebrates the power of God who looses barrenness, and honors the holy ancestors of Christ. It stands within the Nativity Fast as a quiet foreshadowing of the salvation prepared for the human race.

12-10.name: Menas, Hermogenes and Eugraphus
12-10.desc: Holy Martyrs Menas, Hermogenes and Eugraphus.
12-10.bio:
The holy martyrs Menas, Hermogenes, and Eugraphus suffered at Alexandria in the early fourth century. Menas, called the Melodious for his eloquence, was sent to the city on imperial business and openly preached Christ there; Hermogenes, sent to judge him, was won to the faith by his endurance and the grace shown in him, and Eugraphus, the companion of Menas, confessed Christ with them. All three were put to death by beheading.

The Church honors them as witnesses whose wisdom and courage turned even their persecutor to Christ. They are commemorated on December 10.

12-11.name: Daniel the Stylite
12-11.bio:
Venerable Daniel the Stylite was a monk of the fifth century who, inspired by the example of St. Symeon the Stylite, took his stand upon a pillar near Constantinople and remained there in prayer for more than thirty years, enduring frost, wind, and burning heat. Emperors and patriarchs climbed to seek his counsel, and he came down only once, to defend the Orthodox faith in the capital.

He reposed in extreme old age, revered by the whole city as an intercessor and guide. He is commemorated on December 11.

12-12.name: Spyridon of Trimythous
12-12.desc: Bishop Spyridon of Tremithus, wonderworker, patron of Corfu.
12-12.bio:
St. Spyridon, Bishop of Trimythous in Cyprus, was a shepherd of great simplicity and holiness who lived in the fourth century. Married and later widowed, he was made bishop while continuing to tend his sheep. According to tradition, at the First Ecumenical Council he demonstrated the unity of the Holy Trinity by pressing a clay tile, from which fire rose, water flowed, and earth remained in his hand.

His incorrupt relics rest on Corfu, whose patron he is, and many miracles are ascribed to his intercession through the centuries. He is commemorated on December 12 and honored with processions on Corfu several times each year.

12-13.name: Eustratius and companions
12-13.bio:
The holy Five Martyrs Eustratius, Auxentius, Eugene, Mardarius, and Orestes suffered for Christ in Armenia during the persecution under Diocletian at the turn of the fourth century. Eustratius, a distinguished imperial officer, confessed Christ openly and endured many torments together with his companions, each of whom sealed his faith with his blood.

The prayer of St. Eustratius, spoken before his death, is read in the Church's midnight service to this day. They are commemorated on December 13.

12-14.name: Thyrsos and companions
12-14.desc: Holy Martyrs Thyrsus, Leucius, and Callinicus.
12-14.bio:
The holy martyrs Thyrsos, Leucius, and Callinicus suffered for Christ in Asia Minor in the third century, during the Roman persecutions. Refusing to offer sacrifice to the idols, they endured torments with steadfast faith and were put to death, their endurance drawing others to confess Christ.

The synaxaria preserve little beyond their faithful witness, which the Church holds in honor among the martyrs of that age. They are commemorated on December 14.

12-15.name: Eleutherios
12-15.bio:
The holy hieromartyr Eleutherios was a bishop of the early Church, raised in piety by his mother Anthia and consecrated to the episcopate while still young. According to tradition he suffered in the persecutions of the second century: brought before the emperor, he refused to deny Christ, endured many torments unharmed, and was finally put to death, his mother Anthia being slain beside him.

His name means freedom, and the faithful ask his intercession for deliverance from every bond; his feast is a beloved name day for Eleftherios and Lefteris. He is commemorated on December 15.

12-16.name: Aggaeus the Prophet
12-16.bio:
The holy prophet Aggaeus, called Haggai in the Hebrew Scriptures, is one of the twelve minor prophets. He prophesied in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian captivity, stirring up the people and their leaders to rebuild the Temple of the Lord, and declaring that the glory of the latter house would surpass the former.

The Church honors him among the prophets whose words looked beyond the earthly Temple to the coming of Christ. He is commemorated on December 16.

12-17.name: Daniel the Prophet
12-17.desc: Holy Prophet Daniel and the Three Holy Youths Ananias, Azarias, Misael.
12-17.bio:
The holy prophet Daniel was carried as a youth into the Babylonian captivity, where he served in the courts of kings without ever compromising his faith. God gave him understanding of dreams and visions of the kingdoms of the world and of the Son of Man; cast into the den of lions for praying to his God, he was preserved unharmed. With him the Church honors the Three Holy Youths, Ananias, Azarias, and Misael, who walked unburned in the fiery furnace rather than worship the golden idol.

Their deliverance is sung in the Church as a figure of the Resurrection and of the Virgin Birth. They are commemorated on December 17.

12-18.name: Sebastian
12-18.bio:
The holy martyr Sebastian was a Roman soldier of high rank who suffered under the persecution of Diocletian at the end of the third century. A secret Christian who strengthened imprisoned confessors, he was denounced, bound to a tree, and shot with arrows; found still living, he confessed Christ again before the emperor and was then put to death. A company of martyrs who suffered with him is honored alongside him.

He is one of the most venerated of the Roman martyrs, in both East and West. He is commemorated on December 18.

12-19.name: Boniface
12-19.bio:
The holy martyr Boniface was a servant of a wealthy Roman woman, Aglais, in the early fourth century. Sent by her to the East to bring back relics of the martyrs, he watched the sufferings of the confessors at Tarsus, was pierced with compunction for his own careless life, and openly declared himself a Christian; he was tortured and beheaded, and his own relics were carried back to Rome, where Aglais received them and thereafter lived in repentance.

His story is treasured as an image of sudden, wholehearted repentance crowned by martyrdom. He is commemorated on December 19.

12-20.name: Ignatius the God-Bearer
12-20.desc: Holy Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer of Antioch.
12-20.bio:
The holy hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer was Bishop of Antioch in the generation after the Apostles, a disciple of the apostolic age who shepherded one of the great churches of the early world. Condemned under the emperor Trajan, he was taken in bonds to Rome, and on the journey wrote seven epistles that remain among the treasures of the early Church, begging the faithful not to hinder his martyrdom; he was given to the wild beasts in the arena.

He called himself the wheat of God, ground by the teeth of beasts to become pure bread of Christ. He is commemorated on December 20.

12-21.name: Juliana of Nicomedia
12-21.bio:
The holy martyr Juliana was a young Christian of Nicomedia who suffered in the persecutions at the beginning of the fourth century. Betrothed to a pagan of rank, she refused to marry him unless he came to Christ, and for her confession she endured imprisonment and cruel tortures with unshaken constancy before being put to death by the sword.

Her courage moved many who witnessed her sufferings to believe, and the Church honors her among the brave virgin martyrs of Nicomedia. She is commemorated on December 21.

12-22.name: Anastasia the Pharmakolytria
12-22.desc: Great Martyr Anastasia the Deliverer from Potions.
12-22.bio:
The great martyr Anastasia was a Roman Christian of noble birth who suffered under the persecution of Diocletian at the turn of the fourth century. She devoted her wealth and freedom to visiting imprisoned Christians, tending their wounds and strengthening them for their contest, until she herself was seized and, after many trials, put to death.

She is called Pharmakolytria, Deliverer from Potions, for the faithful seek her protection against poisons, spells, and every harmful thing. She is commemorated on December 22.

12-23.name: Ten Martyrs of Crete
12-23.desc: The Ten Holy Martyrs of Crete.
12-23.bio:
The Ten Holy Martyrs of Crete suffered together under the persecution of the emperor Decius in the third century. Drawn from various towns of the island, they were brought before the governor at Gortyna, and when they refused to sacrifice to the idols they endured mockery and torments for many days before being beheaded, going to their death rejoicing.

They are the boast of the Church of Crete, which honors them as its own firstfruits among the martyrs. They are commemorated on December 23.

12-25.name: Nativity of Christ
12-25.desc: The Nativity of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ.
12-25.bio:
The Nativity of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ, kept on December 25, celebrates the birth in the flesh of the Son of God from the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem. Laid in a manger because there was no room at the inn, the newborn King was glorified by angels, worshipped by shepherds, and honored with gifts by Magi from the East.

Christmas is, after Pascha, the greatest feast of the church year, prepared by a forty-day fast. In the Child of Bethlehem the Church confesses God become man, that man might be brought back to God.

12-26.name: Synaxis of the Theotokos
12-26.desc: Synaxis of the Most Holy Theotokos — day after Nativity.
12-26.bio:
On the day after the Nativity of Christ, the Church gathers in synaxis to honor the Most Holy Theotokos, from whom the Saviour was born in the flesh. Having celebrated the birth of the Lord, the faithful turn with gratitude to His Mother, through whose obedience the Incarnation came to pass.

This is among the most ancient feasts of the Mother of God, and it follows a pattern kept throughout the church year, in which the day after a Great Feast honors the principal servant of the mystery. The synaxis proclaims Mary truly Theotokos, the Birth-giver of God.

12-26.name: King David, Joseph, James
12-26.desc: Sunday after Nativity — Synaxis of Joseph, David the Prophet, and James.
12-26.bio:
On the Sunday after the Nativity the Church keeps the synaxis of three holy kinsmen of the Lord according to the flesh: David the Prophet and King, from whose line the Messiah was born; Joseph the Betrothed, the righteous elder who guarded the Virgin and the Christ Child and led them to safety in Egypt; and James the Brother of the Lord, first Bishop of Jerusalem.

The feast honors those bound most closely to the mystery of the Incarnation by kinship and faithful service. It is kept on the Sunday after the Nativity, commemorated in this calendar on December 26.

12-27.name: Stephen the First Martyr
12-27.bio:
St. Stephen, the Protomartyr and Archdeacon, was one of the seven deacons chosen by the Apostles to serve the first church in Jerusalem. Full of grace and power, he preached Christ boldly; accused before the council, he beheld the heavens opened and the Son of Man at the right hand of God, and was stoned to death, praying for his slayers, while the young Saul, the future Apostle Paul, stood by.

He is the first martyr of the Church, and his witness became the pattern for all martyrs after him. His feast is kept on December 27, within the days of the Nativity.

12-28.name: Twenty Thousand Martyrs of Nicomedia
12-28.desc: The Twenty Thousand Holy Martyrs of Nicomedia.
12-28.bio:
The Twenty Thousand Holy Martyrs of Nicomedia suffered at the beginning of the fourth century, in the great persecution under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. According to tradition, a vast multitude of Christians had gathered in the church of Nicomedia for the feast of the Nativity when the building was surrounded; commanded to sacrifice to the idols, they refused as one, and the church was set alight, the faithful within perishing in the flames with prayer on their lips.

The Church honors them as a whole congregation crowned together. They are commemorated on December 28.

12-31.name: Melania the Elder
12-31.desc: Venerable Melania the Elder of Rome.
12-31.bio:
St. Melania was a Roman noblewoman of one of the wealthiest families of the empire who, in the era of the great flowering of monasticism, renounced rank and riches for the sake of Christ. She gave her vast possessions to the poor and to the churches, freed those enslaved to her household, and devoted herself to asceticism, prayer, and the service of the monks and holy places of the East, ending her days in the Holy Land.

She is honored as a model of voluntary poverty embraced out of love for God. She is commemorated on December 31.

2-22.name: Athanasius the Confessor
2-22.bio:
St. Athanasius the Confessor was a monk who lived in the time of the iconoclast persecutions, when the emperors made war upon the holy images. For his steadfast veneration of the icons of Christ and His saints he endured affliction and persecution, bearing witness to the Orthodox faith without wavering.

Having confessed the truth to the end, he reposed in peace, and the Church numbers him among the confessors who preserved the veneration of the holy icons. He is commemorated on February 22.

2-24.name: Finding of the Head of St. John the Baptist
2-24.desc: First and Second Finding of the Honorable Head of the Holy Forerunner.
2-24.bio:
This feast commemorates the First and Second Findings of the honorable head of St. John the Forerunner. According to tradition, after the Baptist was beheaded by Herod his head was hidden, and in later generations it was revealed and recovered by the faithful; in times of persecution it was concealed again and found anew, each recovery received with rejoicing and accompanied by healings.

The Church keeps this commemoration on February 24, honoring the relics of the greatest of the prophets. The feast bears witness to the Orthodox veneration of holy relics, through which the grace of God that dwelt in the saints continues to work.

2-28.name: Basil the Confessor
2-28.desc: Venerable Basil the Confessor, companion of St. Procopius.
2-28.bio:
St. Basil the Confessor was a monk of the eighth century and the companion in asceticism of St. Prokopios of the Dekapolis. When the iconoclast heresy broke out, he stood with his fellow ascetic in defense of the veneration of the holy icons, and for this confession he endured imprisonment and ill-treatment.

When the persecution abated he returned to his labors of fasting and prayer, guiding others in the ascetic life until his peaceful repose. He is commemorated on February 28.

2-29.name: John Cassian the Roman
2-29.bio:
St. John Cassian the Roman was a monk of the late fourth and early fifth centuries. In his youth he journeyed with his friend Germanos to the monasteries of Palestine and to the great elders of the Egyptian desert, gathering their wisdom, and later he settled in Gaul, near Marseilles, where he founded monasteries for men and for women.

His writings, the Institutes and the Conferences, carried the teaching of the desert fathers to the Christian West and remain classics of the spiritual life. His memory is kept on February 29, and in ordinary years on February 28.

3-7.name: Ephraim, Bishop of Cherson
3-7.desc: Holy Hieromartyrs and Bishops of Cherson.
3-7.bio:
St. Ephraim was one of the holy bishops sent in the early fourth century to preach the Gospel in Cherson on the Black Sea, a region still in the grip of paganism. Together with his fellow hieromartyr bishops of Cherson, he labored to plant the faith among a hostile people, and sealed his preaching with his blood.

The Church remembers these missionary bishops together as founders of the Church in that land, their sacrifice bearing fruit in generations of believers. St. Ephraim is commemorated on March 7.

3-16.name: Christodoulos of Patmos
3-16.bio:
St. Christodoulos was a monk of the eleventh century, born in Asia Minor, who lived the ascetic life in various monasteries of the East before receiving from the emperor the island of Patmos, where St. John received the Revelation. There he founded the great Monastery of St. John the Theologian, which crowns the island to this day.

Honored as a wonderworker in his lifetime and after his repose, he made Patmos one of the enduring lamps of Orthodox monasticism. His relics rest at his monastery, and he is commemorated on March 16.

3-24.name: Artemon, Bishop of Seleucia
3-24.bio:
St. Artemon is honored as one of the earliest bishops of the Church, shepherd of Seleucia in Asia Minor in apostolic times. Tradition associates him with the first generation of those who received the Gospel from the Apostles and gave their lives to establishing the Church among the pagans.

The synaxaria preserve little of his life beyond his faithful episcopal service, but his memory endures as one of the quiet founders on whom the Church was built. He is commemorated on March 24.

3-26.name: Synaxis of the Archangel Gabriel
3-26.desc: Synaxis of the Holy Archangel Gabriel, the day after the Annunciation.
3-26.bio:
On the day after the Annunciation, the Church gathers in synaxis to honor the Archangel Gabriel, the messenger of the Incarnation. It was Gabriel who announced the conception of St. John the Forerunner to Zacharias, and above all who brought the Virgin Mary the good tidings that she would bear the Saviour of the world.

In Scripture and tradition Gabriel appears at the turning points of salvation history as the herald of divine mysteries. The faithful seek his intercession as one of the chief commanders of the heavenly hosts, honored again with the Archangel Michael on November 8.

3-27.name: Matrona of Thessaloniki
3-27.bio:
St. Matrona was a servant in Thessaloniki in the early centuries of the Church, a Christian in the household of a pagan-hearted mistress who hated her faith. Slipping away in secret to pray with the Church, she was discovered, beaten, and confined, yet she would not abandon Christ, and she died of the cruel treatment she received, a true martyr.

The Christians of Thessaloniki honored her from ancient times, and her memory endures as a witness that no station in life is too lowly for sanctity. She is commemorated on March 27.

3-28.name: Hilarion the New
3-28.desc: Venerable Hilarion the New, Abbot of Pelekete.
3-28.bio:
St. Hilarion the New was abbot of the monastery of Pelekete in Asia Minor during the age of iconoclasm. A man of fasting, vigil, and deep humility, he guided his brotherhood in the monastic life and stood firm in the veneration of the holy icons when the emperors sought to abolish it.

For this confession he and his monastery suffered persecution, and he is numbered among the confessors who preserved the fullness of the faith for the generations after them. He is commemorated on March 28.

3-29.name: Mark, Bishop of Arethusa
3-29.bio:
St. Mark was Bishop of Arethusa in Syria in the fourth century. In the days of Constantine he had destroyed a pagan temple and built up the Church; when Julian the Apostate restored idolatry, the aged bishop was seized by the pagans of the city and subjected to prolonged and vicious torments, which he endured with such meekness that even his tormentors marveled.

His patience under suffering became famous throughout the Church, and the fathers held him up as a model of forgiveness toward persecutors. He is commemorated on March 29.

3-30.name: John Climacus
3-30.desc: Venerable John Climacus, author of The Ladder of Divine Ascent.
3-30.bio:
St. John Climacus came to Mount Sinai as a young man and spent his whole life there, first in obedience to an elder, then in long years of stillness in the desert, and finally as abbot of the great monastery of Sinai. At the request of another abbot he wrote The Ladder of Divine Ascent, describing thirty steps of the spiritual life leading from renunciation to love.

The Ladder became one of the most beloved books of Orthodox spirituality, read in monasteries every Great Lent. He is commemorated on March 30 and on the fourth Sunday of the Fast.

3-31.name: Hypatius, Bishop of Gangra
3-31.desc: Hieromartyr Hypatius the Wonderworker, Bishop of Gangra.
3-31.bio:
St. Hypatius was Bishop of Gangra in Paphlagonia in the fourth century and a father of the First Ecumenical Council at Nicaea, where the divinity of Christ was confessed against Arius. A wonderworker famed for his prayers, he shepherded his flock with zeal against every heresy.

Tradition relates that he was ambushed by heretics on a mountain road and mortally wounded, dying with prayer for his attackers, so that the Church honors him as both hierarch and martyr. He is commemorated on March 31.

4-2.name: Titus the Wonderworker
4-2.bio:
St. Titus the Wonderworker was a monk who from his youth gave himself to the ascetic life, excelling in obedience, humility, and love for the brethren. He served Christ in a monastic brotherhood, and for the purity of his life he received from God the grace of working wonders, from which he takes his title.

The synaxaria preserve few details of his story, but the Church keeps his memory as one of the quiet venerable fathers whose hidden labors adorned the monastic life. He is commemorated on April 2.

4-3.name: Nicetas the Confessor
4-3.desc: Venerable Nicetas the Confessor, Abbot of Medikion.
4-3.bio:
St. Nicetas the Confessor was abbot of the monastery of Medikion in Bithynia in the late eighth and early ninth centuries. A gentle father to his monks, he guided his community in prayer and asceticism until the renewal of iconoclasm, when he refused to reject the holy icons and was imprisoned and exiled by the emperor.

He endured his sufferings with patience and reposed a confessor, honored throughout the Church for his steadfastness in the Orthodox faith. He is commemorated on April 3.

4-7.name: George of Mytilene
4-7.desc: St. George the Confessor, Bishop of Mytilene.
4-7.bio:
St. George the Confessor was Bishop of Mytilene on the island of Lesbos during the age of iconoclasm. A merciful shepherd known for his almsgiving and ascetic life, he refused to abandon the veneration of the holy icons when the emperors demanded it, and in his old age he was driven from his see into exile, where he ended his days.

The faithful of Lesbos have honored him from ancient times among their chief intercessors. He is commemorated on April 7.

4-14.name: Martin the Confessor, Pope of Rome
4-14.desc: Hieromartyr Martin the Confessor, Pope of Rome.
4-14.bio:
St. Martin, Pope of Rome, was one of the great confessors of the seventh century. When the Monothelite heresy, supported by the imperial court, denied the fullness of Christ's human will, Martin gathered a council at the Lateran which condemned the error. The emperor's men seized the ailing pope, brought him in chains to Constantinople, and after a humiliating trial banished him to distant Cherson.

There, abandoned and deprived of necessities, he died for the faith he would not compromise. He is commemorated on April 14.

4-15.name: Apostles Aristarchus, Pudens & Trophimus
4-15.desc: Holy Apostles of the Seventy: Aristarchus, Pudens, and Trophimus.
4-15.bio:
The holy Apostles Aristarchus, Pudens, and Trophimus were of the Seventy, fellow laborers of the Apostle Paul who are named in his epistles. Aristarchus shared Paul's journeys and imprisonment; Pudens received the faithful into his house in Rome; Trophimus accompanied Paul on his travels and shared his final trials.

According to tradition, all three completed their apostolic course as martyrs in Rome in the days of Nero, beheaded for the name of Christ. They are commemorated together on April 15.

4-16.name: Irene, Agape & Chionia
4-16.desc: Holy Martyrs Agape, Irene, and Chionia.
4-16.bio:
The holy virgins Agape, Irene, and Chionia were sisters from the region of Thessaloniki who suffered in the year 304, during the persecution of Diocletian. Arrested for their faith and for keeping the holy Scriptures when the emperor had ordered them destroyed, they refused to eat food sacrificed to idols or deny Christ, standing firm through interrogation.

Agape and Chionia were burned, and Irene, after further trials, followed her sisters in martyrdom. Three sisters crowned as one, they are commemorated on April 16.

4-18.name: Cosmas, Bishop of Chalcedon
4-18.desc: St. Cosmas the Confessor, Bishop of Chalcedon.
4-18.bio:
St. Cosmas the Confessor was Bishop of Chalcedon in the ninth century, during the second period of iconoclasm. Raised in the monastic life before his consecration, he refused to renounce the veneration of the holy icons when the emperor demanded it, and for this he was stripped of his see and endured persecution and exile.

He remained faithful to the end, and the Church numbers him among the confessor hierarchs through whom the Orthodox faith was preserved. He is commemorated on April 18.

4-20.name: Theodore Trichinas
4-20.desc: Venerable Theodore Trichinas, the Hair-shirt Wearer.
4-20.bio:
St. Theodore Trichinas was born in Constantinople and embraced the monastic life in a monastery of the countryside. He is called Trichinas, the hair-shirt wearer, because his only garment throughout his long ascetic struggle was a rough covering of hair, worn in every season as he mortified the flesh through fasting, vigil, and cold.

God glorified his hidden labors with the grace of wonders, and after his repose the faithful continued to receive healing at his relics. He is commemorated on April 20.

4-27.name: Simeon, Bishop of Jerusalem
4-27.desc: Hieromartyr Simeon, Kinsman of the Lord, Bishop of Jerusalem.
4-27.bio:
St. Simeon was a kinsman of the Lord according to the flesh, the son of Clopas, and became the second Bishop of Jerusalem after the death of James the Brother of God. He shepherded the mother Church of Jerusalem through decades of trial, including the destruction of the city, guarding the flock of Christ in the very places of His Passion and Resurrection.

In extreme old age he was denounced to the Romans, and after enduring tortures was crucified in the days of the emperor Trajan, following his Lord in the manner of his death. He is commemorated on April 27.

4-28.name: Apostles Jason & Sosipater
4-28.desc: Holy Apostles of the Seventy Jason and Sosipater.
4-28.bio:
The holy Apostles Jason and Sosipater were of the Seventy, kinsmen and fellow laborers of the Apostle Paul, who greets them in his Epistle to the Romans. According to tradition they carried the Gospel to the island of Kerkyra, where they preached, endured imprisonment, and converted many to Christ, including members of the ruling house.

They are honored as the founders and enlighteners of the Church of Corfu, where their veneration has continued unbroken since ancient times. They are commemorated together on April 28.

4-29.name: Nine Martyrs of Cyzicus
4-29.desc: The Holy Nine Martyrs of Cyzicus.
4-29.bio:
The holy Nine Martyrs suffered at Cyzicus, a city on the southern shore of the Sea of Marmara, during the persecutions of the third century. Christians of different ages and walks of life, they confessed Christ openly before the authorities, and when neither threats nor torments could move them, all nine were beheaded together.

When peace came to the Church their relics were found incorrupt, and a church was raised over them; many healings were received there by the faithful. They are commemorated on April 29.

4-30.name: James the Apostle, Son of Zebedee
4-30.desc: Holy Apostle James, son of Zebedee, brother of John the Theologian.
4-30.bio:
St. James, the son of Zebedee and elder brother of St. John the Theologian, was called by the Lord from his father's fishing boat to become one of the Twelve. With Peter and John he belonged to the innermost circle of the disciples, present at the Transfiguration and at the agony in Gethsemane.

As the Acts of the Apostles records, he was the first of the Twelve to drink the cup of martyrdom, beheaded in Jerusalem by Herod Agrippa. The Church honors him as the protomartyr among the apostles, and commemorates him on April 30.

5-11.name: Mocius the Martyr
5-11.desc: Hieromartyr Mocius, patron of the founding of Constantinople.
5-11.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Mocius was a priest who suffered for Christ at the beginning of the fourth century, during the persecution of Diocletian. Preaching boldly against the worship of idols, he was arrested and endured many torments, and was finally beheaded at Byzantium, faithful to the end.

He was venerated in that city from early times, and St. Constantine the Great raised a great church in his honor in the new capital. His feast on May 11 coincides with the day Constantinople was dedicated, and he is remembered as one of the city's heavenly protectors.

5-18.name: Theodotus of Ancyra
5-18.desc: Holy Martyr Theodotus of Ancyra and the Seven Virgins.
5-18.bio:
The Holy Martyr Theodotus of Ancyra suffered under the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. An innkeeper by trade, he secretly aided the persecuted Christians of the city; when seven holy virgins of Ancyra were put to death for their faith, tradition tells that Theodotus recovered their bodies and gave them burial, though it was forbidden on pain of death. For this he was seized, tortured, and beheaded.

He is commemorated together with the Seven Virgins of Ancyra on May 18, a witness that mercy toward the martyrs is itself a crown.

5-19.name: Patrick, Bishop of Prusa
5-19.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Patrick was Bishop of Prusa in Bithynia in the early centuries of the Church. Brought before the pagan governor with priests of his church, he confessed Christ as the Creator of all, refusing to ascribe the works of God to the idols, and for his boldness he was put to death by the sword together with his companions.

The Church honors him among the shepherd-martyrs who taught the truth with their words and sealed it with their blood. He is commemorated on May 19.

5-20.name: Lydia of Philippi
5-20.desc: St. Lydia of Philippi, the first European convert of the Apostle Paul.
5-20.bio:
St. Lydia of Philippi holds a beloved place in the Church as the first person baptized by the Apostle Paul on European soil. A seller of purple goods from Thyatira, she was a devout worshipper of God, and as she listened to Paul by the riverside at Philippi the Lord opened her heart to receive the Gospel. She was baptized with her whole household and welcomed the Apostles into her home.

Her hospitality made her house the first gathering place of the church at Philippi, and she is honored as Equal-to-the-Apostles in Greek tradition. She is commemorated on May 20.

5-27.name: John the Russian
5-27.desc: St. John the Russian, Confessor, of Evia.
5-27.bio:
St. John the Russian was a soldier taken captive during the wars between Russia and the Ottoman Empire early in the eighteenth century, and sold into slavery in Prokopi of Asia Minor. Refusing to abandon his faith, he served his master humbly, living in a stable in prayer and fasting, and came to be revered even by his captors as a man of God.

He reposed in 1730, and his incorrupt relics were brought with the Asia Minor refugees in 1924 to New Prokopi on the island of Evia, where his shrine is one of the great pilgrimage centers of Greece. His feast is May 27.

5-31.name: Hermias the Martyr
5-31.bio:
The Holy Martyr Hermias was an aged soldier who suffered for Christ at Comana in the second century. Summoned in his old age to sacrifice to the idols, the veteran refused, confessing the Lord whom he had served all his life, and he endured many torments with a young man's courage before being put to death by the sword.

The Church honors in him the crown of a long life made perfect in martyrdom, and in Greece his feast is kept as the name day of those called Ermis. He is commemorated on May 31.

6-9.name: Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria
6-9.desc: St. Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria, Pillar of Orthodoxy.
6-9.bio:
St. Cyril was Archbishop of Alexandria in the fifth century and one of the great theologians of the Church. When Nestorius denied that the Virgin Mary may be called Theotokos, Birth-Giver of God, Cyril rose in defense of the truth that the one born of her is truly God the Word made flesh. He presided at the Third Ecumenical Council at Ephesus in 431, which upheld the Orthodox faith.

Called the Pillar of Orthodoxy, he reposed in 444, leaving writings that remain foundations of the Church's teaching on Christ. He is commemorated on June 9, and with St. Athanasios on January 18.

6-10.name: Timothy, Bishop of Prusa
6-10.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Timothy was Bishop of Prusa in Bithynia in the fourth century, a shepherd of holy life to whom tradition ascribes the grace of wonderworking. In the days of Julian the Apostate, when the emperor sought to restore the worship of idols, Timothy would not cease preaching Christ, and for his boldness he was imprisoned and put to death.

The Church honors him among the hieromartyrs who withstood the last pagan reaction of the empire, faithful shepherds who chose death over silence. He is commemorated on June 10.

6-19.name: Apostle Jude, Brother of the Lord
6-19.desc: Holy Apostle Jude (Thaddeus), Brother of the Lord.
6-19.bio:
The Holy Apostle Jude, called Thaddeus, is numbered among the Twelve and is known as the Brother of the Lord, being of the household of the righteous Joseph. He wrote the short catholic epistle that bears his name, urging the faithful to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. After Pentecost he preached the Gospel in the lands of the East, and tradition holds that he ended his labors as a martyr.

The Church honors him as apostle, kinsman of the Lord according to the flesh, and witness unto blood. He is commemorated on June 19.

6-19.name: John Maximovitch of Shanghai
6-19.desc: St. John Maximovitch, Wonderworker and Archbishop of Shanghai and San Francisco.
6-19.bio:
St. John Maximovitch, Archbishop of Shanghai and San Francisco, was one of the great saints of the twentieth century. Born in Russia in 1896, he served as bishop in Shanghai, where he sheltered orphans and the poor, and later shepherded his scattered flock in Western Europe and America. A strict ascetic who served the Divine Liturgy daily, he was known even in his lifetime as a wonderworker whose prayers brought healing.

He reposed in 1966 while accompanying a wonderworking icon of the Mother of God, and his relics rest in San Francisco. Glorified in 1994, he is honored on this day as a wonderworker of the latter times.

6-20.name: Methodius, Bishop of Patara
6-20.bio:
The Holy Hieromartyr Methodius was Bishop of Patara in Lycia at the turn of the fourth century. A learned shepherd and one of the notable church writers of his age, he defended the resurrection of the body and the purity of the faith, and composed works in praise of virginity. In the last great persecution he was seized for his confession of Christ and put to death by the sword.

The Church honors him as a teacher who served the truth with both pen and blood. He is commemorated on June 20.

6-28.name: Sts. Cyrus & John the Unmercenaries
6-28.desc: Translation of the relics of the Holy Unmercenaries Cyrus and John.
6-28.bio:
On June 28 the Church commemorates the translation of the relics of the Holy Unmercenaries Cyrus and John. Cyrus was a physician of Alexandria who healed in the name of Christ without payment, and John a soldier who joined him; together they strengthened the confessors during the persecution of Diocletian and were beheaded for the faith at the beginning of the fourth century.

In the fifth century their relics were translated with honor to Menouthis near Alexandria, where countless healings were wrought and the last strongholds of paganism gave way. Their principal feast is kept on January 31, and the translation of their relics on June 28.

7-13.name: Stephen the Sabbaite
7-13.bio:
St. Stephen the Sabbaite was a monk of the renowned Lavra of St. Savas in the Judean desert, living in the eighth century. Given to the monastery from childhood, he grew up in its life of prayer, was formed in its discipline, and spent his years in ascetic struggle, stillness, and love for the brethren, becoming a spiritual guide to many.

He is remembered also as a hymnographer of the Church, in the great tradition of the Lavra that nurtured him. He reposed in peace and is commemorated on July 13.

7-13.name: Synaxis of the Archangel Gabriel
7-13.desc: Second Synaxis of the Holy Archangel Gabriel, chief of the Bodiless Powers.
7-13.bio:
On July 13 the Church keeps a second synaxis in honor of the Archangel Gabriel, gathering the faithful once more to celebrate the great messenger of God. Tradition connects the feast with the dedication of a church in his name and with thanksgiving for his wonders through the centuries.

Gabriel is honored as the herald of the Incarnation, who brought the good tidings to the Theotokos, and as one of the chief commanders of the bodiless powers who stand before the throne of God. He is honored also on March 26 and, with the Archangel Michael, on November 8.

7-31.name: Eudokimos the Righteous
7-31.desc: St. Eudokimos the Righteous of Cappadocia.
7-31.bio:
St. Eudokimos the Righteous was born in Cappadocia in the ninth century to devout parents. Serving as an officer in the imperial service, he lived in the midst of the world a life of hidden holiness, guarding purity, giving alms generously to the poor and to widows and orphans, and avoiding all display, with a special reverence for the Theotokos.

He reposed while still young, and God glorified his hidden virtue, for his relics were found incorrupt and wrought healings. His name means one of good repute, and he is commemorated on July 31.

8-2.name: Translation of Relics of St. Stephen
8-2.desc: Translation of the relics of the Holy Protomartyr Stephen.
8-2.bio:
This feast commemorates the translation of the relics of the Holy Protomartyr and Archdeacon Stephen, the first to shed his blood for Christ, stoned outside Jerusalem as recorded in the Acts of the Apostles. According to tradition, his long-hidden relics were revealed in the fifth century and were later brought with great honor to Constantinople, where the faithful received them with rejoicing.

Through his relics many healings were granted, and the Church glorifies God who is wondrous in His saints. The translation is commemorated on August 2; his principal feast is December 27.

8-12.name: Martyrs Photius & Anicetas
8-12.desc: Holy Martyrs Photius and Anicetas of Nicomedia.
8-12.bio:
Sts. Photius and Anicetas were martyrs of Nicomedia who suffered during the persecution of Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century. According to tradition they were kinsmen; Anicetas confessed Christ boldly before the emperor, and Photius embraced him and followed him in his confession. Together they endured imprisonment and many torments, and were finally put to death by fire, receiving together the crown of martyrdom.

Their shared steadfastness has been honored through the centuries, and those named Photios and Fotis keep their name day in their memory. They are commemorated on August 12.

8-14.name: Micah the Prophet
8-14.bio:
The Holy Prophet Micah was one of the twelve minor prophets, prophesying in the kingdom of Judah in the eighth century before Christ, in the days of the Prophet Isaiah. He rebuked injustice and false worship, foretold judgment upon Jerusalem, and proclaimed the mercy of God who pardons iniquity.

Above all he is remembered for foretelling that from Bethlehem would come forth the Ruler of Israel, the prophecy fulfilled in the Nativity of Christ. He is commemorated on August 14.

10-23.name: Ignatius, Patriarch of Constantinople
10-23.bio:
St. Ignatius was Patriarch of Constantinople in the ninth century. The son of an emperor, he was tonsured a monk in his youth after his father's fall from power, and rose by his virtue to the patriarchal throne, which he occupied twice amid the turbulence of imperial politics, suffering deposition and exile for his firmness.

He bore his trials with patience and forgiveness, and ended his days in peace, honored for his ascetic life and his steadfastness as a shepherd of the Church. He is commemorated on October 23.

12-24.name: Eugenia of Rome
12-24.desc: Holy Virgin-martyr Eugenia of Rome, on the Eve of the Nativity.
12-24.bio:
The holy virgin martyr Eugenia was the daughter of a distinguished Roman family in the third century. Coming to faith in Christ, according to tradition she fled a life of privilege, entered monastic life disguised as a man, and became known for holiness and healing; after many trials, in which her identity and her innocence were revealed, she returned to Rome and was put to death for the faith in the persecutions of that age.

Her feast falls on the eve of the Nativity, joining her witness to the light of the coming feast. She is commemorated on December 24.

12-29.name: Holy Innocents of Bethlehem
12-29.desc: The 14,000 Holy Innocents slain by Herod in Bethlehem.
12-29.bio:
The Holy Innocents are the young children of Bethlehem and its borders slain by King Herod, who, fearing the newborn King announced by the Magi, ordered the death of all the male children of two years and under. The Gospel sees in their death the fulfillment of the prophecy of Rachel weeping for her children, and the Church numbers them by tradition at fourteen thousand.

They are honored as the first blood shed for Christ, infants crowned as martyrs before they could speak. They are commemorated on December 29.

12-30.name: Anysia of Thessaloniki
12-30.bio:
The holy virgin martyr Anysia was a young Christian of Thessaloniki who lived at the turn of the fourth century, in the days of the persecution under Diocletian. Left wealthy by her parents, she gave her goods to the poor and lived in prayer and quietness. On her way to the gathering of the faithful she was stopped by a soldier who tried to drag her to a pagan sacrifice; when she confessed Christ and resisted, he ran her through with his sword.

She is honored as one of the beloved martyrs of Thessaloniki. She is commemorated on December 30.
